The *Śaivasiddhāntaparibhāṣāmañjarī*,
composed by Nigama-jñānaśivācārya.
Introduction to the *Śaivasiddhāntaparibhāṣāmañjarī*.
I bow to the Lord of Obstacles at Kalpaka, who dwells in the western gate;
he is satisfied by the offering of fruits and is the cause of satisfaction for those who desire their goals.
I worship the illustrious Lord of Tillavana, who is equal to Indra,
and the Daughter of the Mountain, whose joyful dance was cherished by her son.
I worship these devotees: Vyāghrapāda, as well as Śeṣa, Svarṇavarman, and the illustrious lord of Vyāghrapura. (3)
The glorious monastery and temple of Apūrṇa, a residence in the city of Vyāghrapura, honored by Śiva-yogins and a source of jewels among the scriptures of the Āgamas.
Known on earth by the name Vighnānta, a teacher of Vedic knowledge,
I remember that Śiva-yogin who knew the secrets of all the Āgamas.
In the Śaka year marked by the elements and the spirits (1458), in the month known as Mandabhāgya (Māgha),
on the third lunar day, the wise one will enter my year.
He, known by the name Devajñāna, who had reached the further shore of the ocean of Śaiva scriptures,
was brought here to the supreme state of liberation by Kālahastīśvara.
One who bears his name [is protected] by the disciple of that virtuous master, through one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, and so forth. (8)
The *Bhāṣāmañjarī* is being narrated with charming expressions and numerical enumerations;
may the virtuous, who are affectionate toward those who seek their refuge, favor this work. (9)
In some places a mere enumeration is taught, and in others it is accompanied by definitions;
that which is seen in the profound knowledge of Śiva does not exist elsewhere.
Thus ends the introduction.
Now we shall state the *Paribhāṣāmañjarī*: "The Lord, free from beginning, middle, and end, pure by nature, omniscient, and perfect—Śiva is to be known thus in the Śiva-āgama. (1)
Immeasurable, indescribable, incomparable, and free from disease;
subtle, all-pervading, eternal, constant, imperishable, and sovereign. || 2 ||
That which is situated above all paths is declared to be the principle of Śiva (śivatatva). Indeed, the power of consciousness (cicchakti), which is inherent in Śiva, is one alone. (3)
That very [power], due to the differentiation of the acts of liberation, is considered the body of Sadāśiva;
by her—though she is one, she takes manifold forms—the entire universe is sustained. (4)
In the same way, Śiva is indeed one, and his Śakti is likewise immutable;
in the matters of dissolution, enjoyment, and authority, those two do not consist of mere limited elements (tanmātra).
For He is indeed one, yet possesses manifold powers; He is the witness of both perception and action, and is tender.
Just as the blackness residing in copper is known to be distinct from it, like a conch shell, so too is [the individual soul] to be understood.
[One should perform] the rite of the sprout, the sacrifice to the site (vāstuyāga), and likewise the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa).
And likewise, the worship of the pavilion, as well as the sacrificial fuel, the enclosing sticks, and the seat-grass.

One person alone should perform the rites beginning with the *praṇītā* water, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), the vessel, the supporting libation (*ādhāra-pariṣecana*), and ending with the mantras for spreading the grass (*paristaraṇa*). || 8 ||
A single preceptor must perform the rites such as the image-consecration (mūrti-homa) and so forth,
provided that the ritual is being conducted by one person alone and without the use of instrumental assistants.
If that [action] were performed by him [the disciple], it would result in a confusion of teachers;
for where there is a contradiction, it arises solely from the deficiency of the instrument.
That ritual must be performed for him by his disciple according to the scriptures;
however, if it is performed by anyone else, there is no doubt that the performer will meet with destruction.
Now, the sequence for the installation of Sakala and the others is stated:
where one performs the installation of the Sahita [deity], one should perform it in a single location. (12)
One should have everything from the sowing of seeds to the final consecration performed by a single preceptor;
otherwise, it must not be done, for the king and the kingdom will perish.
Thus ends the first chapter.
Now begins the second section.
Two types of Brahman have been pointed out: the Śabdabrahman and that which is the Supreme (Parabrahman). The Supreme is designated as Śiva, expressed by the word "Brahman. || 1 ||
That which consists of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman) is remembered as Sadāśiva;
O Janārdana, the Praṇava is the direct mantra of Sadāśiva.
This Sadāśiva, the God of gods, has become the cause of all;
yet that Supreme Śiva exists as the cause even of him.
Because his nature transcends speech and mind, he is described as the Supreme;
therefore, he who is the causal source is remembered here as Śiva.
Brahman is indeed one and non-dual, yet it is described as being of two kinds;
furthermore, by way of the division into the higher and the lower, it is again twofold.
The Śabdabrahman is praised as being both worldly and Vedic;
and the supreme [Śabdabrahman] is said to be of two kinds: that with qualities (saguṇa) and that which is pure (śuddha). || 6 ||
The limb of Brahmā is both gross and subtle;
the subtle form is declared to be Śiva, while the gross form is Sadāśiva.
O Brahmins, agency is of two kinds: from volition and also from the instrument. A pot is not made by potters through volition alone.
Merely by the thought of Śiva, he is always the agitator of the *bindu*;
yet he possesses no instrument (*karaṇa*), nor is his power (*śakti*) insentient.
Due to the restriction of objects, there is one cognizer;
at that time, it is traditionally known as the two powers: the power of knowledge and the power of action.
Through the power of knowledge he perceives, and through the power of action he creates the world;
first is the creation of Śiva, and second is the creation of the bound souls (paśu).
That which is endowed with a pure body is declared to be the creation of Śiva;
that pure self enveloped by impurities is proclaimed as the creation of the bound soul (paśu).
From Māyā, a twofold creation is proclaimed: the gross and the subtle. The former manifests vision and action; it is real and consists of the common world-elements. || 13 ||
Time should be known as twofold, characterized as gross and subtle;
the gross is said to be worldly, while the subtle belongs to the yogis who possess a variegated nature.
Knowledge is declared to be twofold: the higher is remembered as that which is beyond speech, while the lower is the supreme scripture known as awakening. (15)
In the beginning, there arose twofold knowledge according to the two divisions of authority;
through the distinction between the higher and the lower, it reveals the purpose of the Lord and the bound soul.
The knowledge that reveals Śiva is remembered as the supreme Śivajñāna;
it is the primordial wisdom of the Vedas, which reveals the meaning of both the bound souls (paśu) and the Lord (paśu-pati). || 17 ||
Just as the eye is distinct in its perception during the night for both humans and bats,
so too is knowledge distinct according to the difference between the higher and the lower.
Knowledge is held to be of two kinds: indirect and direct.
They say that indirect knowledge is stationary, while direct knowledge is firmly established. (19)
That which is to be reached at the feet of Maheśa and which proceeds as something indirect shall become direct through the practice [of yoga] under the best of sages. || 20 ||
The object of experience consisting of karma for the bound soul (paśu) is twofold, having the nature of merit and demerit;
one should know that which abides as latent disposition (ābhoga) and is opposed to the two types of fruits.
That conduct is said to be twofold: gross and likewise subtle.
Know that the subtle consists of the spheres (golaka), which are the means for accomplishing both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Birth and death indeed arise from that which is born;
thus has the gross body been described by me in brief. (23)
(7) I shall state the definition of the subtle [principle]; listen to it in brief according to reality.
For every individual, the reality is fixed, beginning with *kalā* and ending with the earth (*avani*). (24)
Like a leech, the soul enters body after body in succession;
having reached a subsequent body by means of its subtle portion, it abandons its former body.
One should cause the yogis to enter the gross and subtle bodies of animals, as well as serpents of the egg-born class, and the various types of wombs. || 26 ||
Abiding in the subtle body as a bound soul (paśu), it then assumes a gross form; through its karma, it remains engaged in the enjoyment of experiences during the states of waking and so forth.
Having thus wandered through all the wombs in succession, one eventually attains human birth, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain, by the power of the passage of time. (28)
Even within the human state, the status of a Brahmin is extremely difficult to attain;
furthermore, the body is said to be of two kinds: that of a male and that of a female. (29)
Masculinity is marked by the *liṅga*, and femininity is marked by the vulva (*yoni*).
The *liṅga* is said to consist of Īśa (Śiva), while the *yoni* is remembered as consisting of Śakti.
Therefore, indeed, this entire world of the moving and the non-moving is Śiva-Śakti;
it exists as a twofold convention, both gross and subtle. || 31 ||
The gross is said to be external, while the subtle is remembered as internal.
Furthermore, there is that which has a support and that which is without support; the one with support belongs to the Sakala [state].

Thus, their initiation is considered to be twofold: that called "without support" (nirādhārā) and [the other]. One should perform it by means of the descent of power (śaktinipāta), which is twofold depending on whether it requires [prior] restraint (nirodha). (33)
In the Kali age, Śiva alone bestows grace upon those who possess realized knowledge until the dissolution;
whatever rite is performed by them is proclaimed to be "without support" (nirādhārā).
Having assumed the form of the Guru, Śambhu performs [the initiation] through his power according to the distinction between mild and intense; that is the initiation which confers authority.
The *kriyāvatī* [initiation] is to be known as twofold: the seedless (*nirbījā*) and the seeded (*sabījikā*). Of these, that which is seedless should be applied to those who have no sons. (36)
Now, there may be initiation with seed (*sabījā*) for both the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the teacher (*ācārya*);
then, initiation without seed (*nirbījikā*) is taught, and it is of two kinds. (37)

The first bestows nirvāṇa immediately; the second, upon the fall of the body. It purifies the web of karma consisting of both that which is currently operative and that which has been accumulated. || 38 ||
Just as it becomes the bestower of immediate nirvāṇa for those who are utterly dispassionate, that [lineage] is divided into two types of seeds; the first is characterized by the nature of Śiva. (39)
That initiation which is conjoined with the cutting of the top-knot is the one characterized by the Dharma of Śiva;
the second, which is purified of mere unrighteousness, is the one characterized by worldly dharma.
For householders, it is to be known as worldly; for those bearing the [ascetic] marks, it is the Śiva-dharma.
There is no cutting of the topknot here; that initiation is characterized by worldly dharma.
(9) Distinction is said to be of two kinds: external and internal.
Birth is indeed said to be of two kinds: initiation and that known as the *praṇava*. 42.
A lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) may initiate both lifelong celibates and householders in due order;
however, a householder who is merely a beginner (bhautika) should not perform the initiation of others.
The supreme teacher is of two kinds: the celibate student (brahmacārī) and the householder (gṛhastha).
Both of these are qualified for initiation (dīkṣā) and consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
But for those disciplined ones whose selves are devoid of worldly power, liberation alone is appropriate;
the student is to be known as the teacher for those seeking both [liberation and worldly success], while the householder is for those seeking both. (45)
The mendicant and the ascetic are not the ones who bestow grace upon the world;
here, equanimity toward actions is not the cause for that grace.
It is indeed like the ripening of a mango fruit; however, as long as that impure power (mālinī-śakti) is joined with devotion to Śiva, it acts as a source of grace.
"Indeed, that [state] which was previously characterized by dullness becomes eternally graced;
just as the individual soul (puruṣa), though pervasive and eternal, having been liberated, attains the state of Śiva.
Thus, even the descent of power (śaktipāta) is spoken of figuratively.
Even this twofold concealment may, in some cases, result in the attainment of a [new] state. || 49 ||
For one established therein, that very same latent impression arises here;
for one endowed with that liberation, there is no conceptualization regarding the self. (50)
By this sequential method, one may attain concealment;
yet for the manifestation of knowledge, each principle (tattva) becomes manifest again and again toward the individual soul (aṇu). (51)
Manifested, he shines like Śiva; indeed, upon the dissolution of the body, he becomes Śiva himself.
In that regard, it is proclaimed to be twofold, consisting of the nature of Śiva and Rudra. (52)
The ten [Tantras] beginning with the Kāmika are proclaimed as the division of Śiva;
the eighteen beginning with the Vijaya are proclaimed as the division of Rudra. (53)
The Śivarudra-tantra consists of twenty-eight Saṃhitās;
each Saṃhitā has four quarters (pādas) and is joined with the Kāmika as its first part.
Thereafter, one should perform the purification of the self, which is proclaimed to be of two kinds;
for the body of the self is what is here designated as the "self. (55)
Regarding those two, purity is as follows: this purity is proclaimed to be the Self.
The body of all embodied beings is composed of the five elements. (56)
Therefore, the purification performed upon them is known as the purification of the body;
for even though the elements remain within this body in a state of friendship, [they must be purified]. (57)
One should conceive of their purification as being established through interruption;
since purity consists of the mantra-nature, one should therefore purify them with the mantra. (58)
Mantra should be understood as being of two forms, distinguished by the categories of the signifier (vācaka) and the signified (vācya).
That which has the form of speech is declared to be the signifier, while that which consists of the object is known as the signified. || 59 ||
And indeed, that which pertains to both the signified and the signifier shall be understood as having that meaning.
One should commence the worship of the Sun either on a small tablet or upon the ground. (60)
For the sake of creation and for the sake of liberation, worship is of two kinds;
indeed, worship is said to be twofold: that which is immobile and that which is mobile. (61)
Established in celestial chariots such as those of the Nāgas and others, that [liṅga] serves the welfare of others;
however, one should worship it constantly when it is mobile, especially for one's own sake. || 62 ||
The worship of Śiva is of two kinds: dependent and independent. Worship of the mobile liṅga is dependent, while that on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) is independent.
Movement is said to be of two kinds: that which has the limbs as its primary focus and that which is directed toward the object itself.
The worship of paintings and the like, as well as of images and the like, takes place before each of those respective objects. (64)

It is said that the limb [of the ritual] has been worshipped; another view considers the principal [limb] to be so. The fire-rite should be known as twofold: either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or even on a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila).
Just as a sacrificial vessel of excellent form is the means for accomplishing all desired objects,
so too is the consecrated ground (sthaṇḍila) the means for all desired objects, especially for the sake of attaining spiritual success (siddhi).
The *liṅga* is said to be of two kinds: the stationary (*sthāvara*) and the moving (*jaṅgama*).
The wise know the stationary *liṅga* to be that which is installed, and the moving one to be the initiated person.
Through the disparagement of the mobile [liṅga], the immobile becomes fruitless;
therefore, a wise person should never disparage either of the two liṅgas. (68)
Having treated [it] with contempt out of delusion, another [result] arises here; of this there is no doubt.
The word *paramaśāyī* (lying supreme) would thus be of two kinds, like the word for "frog. (69)
The frog-shaped and the Devamāna [layout] for a dwelling shall bring auspiciousness;
likewise, the Devī and Vāstu [layouts] provide supreme comfort for sleep.
If it is performed erroneously, the king and the kingdom perish.
The abode of the Child (Bālālaya) is said to be of two kinds: the first and the second. (71)
Whether in a village, a city, a town, or a capital,
or in any other such regions as existed in the past at the original site.

At the conclusion of the instruction on the site, the first [ritual] should be performed. Furthermore, it should be done when constructing a palace, or when it is broken, shattered, or renovated. (73)
Furthermore, that which is performed upon a pedestal (pīṭha), a linga, or images during their separation [from the original] is called the second type, the excellent Taruṇālaya.
Others, however, state that all rites are common;
the second type should be performed without regard to months, fortnights, and so forth. (75)
This is to be known as the second [type]; its tenfold division is understood by the wise:
in a sword, in the original image, in a mirror, and in a reflection; || 76 ||
One should take up the image of the Child (Bālabimba) in a water-pot, on a sacrificial mound, on a mandala, on sandals, or on a cloth painting or a mural. || 77 ||
Whether it be on a self-manifested linga, or one produced by the gods, or one made by sages, or even one made by the Gaṇas, or one made of metal, or at river sources, springs, and the like; (78)
In such signs as these, the stability of the jar [of life] does not occur at all;
however, if [the signs appear] within seven days, or within a fortnight, or within a month, there is stability of the jar.
If the Lord of Gods remains in the water-pot beyond that time, he causes all defects;
five days are declared to be best, while seven days would be middling.
The wise one should declare that the month is the youngest [vessel], and having placed it in a jar,
he should always add fresh water and worship it according to the previous sequence.
Or one should lead the young Gaurī to the upper chamber of the Kāma-kostha; or else, one should install her in the form of a child within the temple of the deity.
One should perform all the rites prescribed in the Vedas as well as those pertaining to the Goddess;
in that regard, a distinction of mantras exists according to the distinction of the ritual acts.
Having performed the worship of Śiva at its conclusion, without the offering of oblations (bali) or fire-sacrifices (homa),
if there is a separate house for the child, one should proceed according to the previously mentioned path of the gods.

Having duly worshipped the Great Goddess with the mantra alone, the preceptor [should perform the rite], provided it is the installation of the Goddess's *bāla* (infant) image in the temple of the Youthful Lord (*taruṇālaya*). 85.
Having completed the temple, the wise man should install Gaurī;
for when neither the God nor the Goddess is present, the deity or the goddess remains alone. (86)

If she is taken by the enemies, then for one who remains [in his position], the other [party] should be brought into conformity; and having established his own foundation, he should bring it to completion. (87)
At the conclusion, the most excellent preceptor should perform this auspicious rite according to the prescribed rules;
for wherever the site of the child is omitted, there is the destruction of sons and grandsons. (88)
Therefore, with every effort, one should fashion the emblem of a child (bālaliṅga).
Hereafter, I shall describe the sacrifice and the fire-oblation following the installation of the Goddess. 89.
Installation is said to be of two kinds: that called ritual action and that which distinguishes yoga.
Having fashioned the deity in sequence along with the Goddess according to the prescribed rule, [one should proceed]. (90)
Where he is established, that is declared to be the installation (sthāpana) of Hari known as the Krama;
having first fashioned the deity together with the Goddess according to the prescribed rite. (91)
Having first installed the God and then the Goddess, even at another time, wherever the Śakti is installed according to the procedure prescribed for installation, [that is a Śaktisthāna]. || 92 ||
That would be the yoga of installation (sthāpana), because it follows immediately after installation;
prior to the installation of Gaurī, there should be the consecration (saṃprokṣaṇa) of Śiva.
Then, having drawn Gaurī from the child’s abode to the temple of Śiva,
the preceptor should place her before the deity in the pavilion according to the previously mentioned procedure.

Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one should thereafter perform auspicious rites. The daily practice is declared to be of two kinds: that which is perpetual and that which is occasional. || 95 ||
One should worship daily every day and perform sacrifice every month;
that which is the special sacrifice is called the "constant" (nitya) tradition.
The occasional rite (naimittika) is to be known as twofold: namely, the occasional and the adventitious.
That which begins with plowing and ends with consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is remembered as the occasional rite.
All other rites are known as occasional (naimittika) and adventitious (āgantuka).
The optional (kāmya) rite is said to be of two kinds: external and internal. || 98 ||
External ritual action is known to bestow supernatural powers (siddhi), while internal action is for one's own spiritual welfare;
this is especially so every year during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
One who desires the two types of accomplishment should worship Śiva at that time;
that worship is to be known as twofold: regular (nitya) and occasional (naimittika). 100.
Indeed, the vow is of two kinds: Vaidika and Śaiva.
The Vaidika form, characterized by the sacred thread (upavīta), is to be performed by those of the three twice-born castes.
The initiation of Śiva is indeed the most important; it is declared to be the supreme Śiva.
Because he was born from the womb of Vāgdevī, he is for that reason the son of Śiva.
For the ten castes beginning with the Brahmins, yoga should be practiced for the sake of attaining excellence;
one should perform what is prescribed in one's own scripture and avoid the scriptures of others.
One should avoid whatever has been stated by others regarding vows, worship, and so forth;
rather, one should grasp therein only that meaning which is not in contradiction with one's own tantra.
16) O Teacher, because of the weakness of their reasoning, that should be understood as a mere mockery of speech;
for wherever, in whatever manner, and by whatever path [it is presented], it is not according to the proper rule. || 105 ||
Whatever can be established here, let that be investigated accordingly;
for if the entire system is of the nature of Śiva, it must be free from all contradiction. (106)
Thus it must be done by the Noble One, and not otherwise, O bull among sages;
for if anything must be performed, that which is contrary to the Śaiva dharma should not be practiced.
If there is a contradiction, it should be abandoned; however, one must not abandon what is Śaiva.
One should accept that which is both Vedic and Śaiva, provided it does not contradict the words of Śiva.
The religious student (brahmacārī) is to be known as twofold: the temporary (bhautika) and the lifelong (naiṣṭhika), the latter being superior.
Upon the completion of his studies and vows, he should follow that [lifelong] path. || 109 ||
The second is declared to be the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika), whose path lasts until the end of the body;
the householder, however, is of two kinds: the indifferent (udāsīna) and the practitioner (sādhaka). (110)
Devoted to the maintenance of his family, this practitioner shall be happy;
having discharged the three debts and renounced wife, wealth, and the like. (111)
He who wanders alone is indifferent and seeks liberation;
yet, among the three stages of life, the householder is said to be their source.
Others depend upon him; therefore, the householder is superior.
For one without a son, the world is empty; for one without a son, whence can there be happiness? (113)
"By means of a son one conquers the worlds; this is the eternal Vedic revelation.
There are two kinds of people who please Śiva: those without wives and those with wives. (114)
Dwelling in the forest, wearing fire-bleached garments, and subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits—such is the vow of the householder, and likewise for him who is accompanied by his wife. (115)
One should constantly practice celibacy, avoiding the acceptance of gifts, whether on level ground, on a patch of earth, on a bed of grass, or on a couch. || 116 ||
One should avoid attachment to all objects of the senses;
having performed ablutions at the three times of day, one should worship the gods, the fire, and the guru. (117)
One should dwell constantly in the forest, subsisting on fruits, roots, and the like;
two states are proclaimed according to the distinction between the pure and the impure. || 118 ||
The states beginning with waking are to be known as twofold, bestowing either the course of worldly existence or liberation.
That which is directed downwards grants worldly existence; that which is directed upwards bestows liberation. (119)
Offense is to be known as twofold: that committed by oneself and that committed by others;
each of these, moreover, is to be known as twofold, according to the distinction between unintentional and intentional. (120)
When the practitioner's own chosen liṅga has been consecrated by another, they say that double the penance must be performed for purification, as if it were one's own work. (121)
For practitioners, the purification of the teacher is considered to be double [that of the practitioner];
for those who have performed the birth-sacrifices, the purification is considered to be double that of materialists.
Light and darkness, as well as the gross and the subtle, likewise the near and the distant, and even that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be accepted. (123)
That which is constant and occasional, the higher and the lower, that which is withdrawn and that which is scattered, as well as the real and the unreal. || 124 ||
"O best of gods, [He is] both being and non-being, likewise the agent and the destroyer;
(the reading is: *saccāsacca suraśreṣṭha kartṛhartṛ tathaiva ca*), and likewise that which is pleasing to the heart and that which is not pleasing to the heart, as well as the future. (125)
That which is the expressed and that which is the expresser, as well as the container and the contained, and that which is called cold and heat, and likewise pleasure and pain; || 126 ||
The pure and the impure, as well as the soft and the sharp;
likewise, the passion and hatred of living beings, as well as diligence and laziness. (127)
Both the elevated and the depressed, as well as success and failure; likewise, the well-established and the ill-established, and both the moving and the immovable. (128)
All this is He alone, the Lord; therefore, nothing else exists apart from Him. || 128½ ||
Thus ends the second chapter.
Now begins the third chapter.
The bound soul (paśu), the fetter (pāśa), and the Lord (pati) are declared to be the three categories.
The bound soul is the self, independent, consisting of pure consciousness, yet defiled by impurities. || 1 ||
That [self] is deluded, eternally transmigrating, possessing limited knowledge, non-divine, and inactive;
whereas the Self is all-pervading, infinite, and remembered as being of the nature of consciousness—these are the two [views]. (2)
According to the distinction between being with all [impurities] or without them, those with one, two, or three impurities are categorized respectively;
he who is severed from the impurities of *māyā* and *karman* is designated as *sakala*. (3)

She is considered "sakala" (with parts) precisely because she possesses the yoga of the eight kalās and so forth; however, he who is enveloped by impurity (mala) and desire (kāma) would be a pralayākala.
Bound by the single bond of impurity (mala), one is called Vijñānakala;
in the world-sphere above the principle of Kalā, liberation may arise for the bound soul (paśu).
Mahāmāyā, Māyā, and Prakṛti in particular—
these three material causes are declared to be its cause.
And that Kuṇḍalinī, the power of Śambhu, though pure and yet of an insentient nature, becomes the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) in three ways: as gross, subtle, and supreme.
That Prakṛti is the mother of the objects of enjoyment, such as the sense organs, for the Puruṣa;
she is the undivided nature of the subtle principles, beginning with time.
She is the mother, the deluding Māyā, the cause of the entire path of purity;
she is the womb of mantra, the supreme Māyā, the eternal Kuṇḍalinī.
(20) Upādāna is the material cause of bodies; Vidya is the cause of those whose nature is that of the Vidyeśvaras.
Śiva is declared to be the agent in the pure path, while Ananta is the Lord in the white [path]. 10.
On the impure path, Rudra is held to be the agent;
he is considered to be threefold, categorized as Sadāśiva, Maheśa, and Rudra.
That which is called the body of Śiva is said to be the body of knowledge (vidyādeha).
That which is known as the Lord (Īśvara) is the instrumental cause, which is perceived together with the material cause.
And that subtle grasping which is joined to all effects—that power which produces the effect, known as action, is of a subtle form. (13)
The gross effect exists within the subtle like the fruit within the seed of a banyan tree;
the subtle [power] resides in the pure path, while the gross resides mixed with the paths.
On the path of impurity (aśuddhādhvan), [the power] Tāpā is situated, which is very gross and stable.
Therein, three words are uttered as feminine, and three meanings are proclaimed. (15)
The path of mantra, the path of word, and the path of phoneme are thus designated;
then, in order, the path of world, the path of principle, and the path of aspect according to their meaning. (16)
Having correctly understood these digits (kalās), which are mixed as gross, subtle, and intermediate,
one understands how the five gross elements are presided over accordingly.
The subtle power (śakti), which pervades all time-periods, exists beyond the world of Sādākhya; in the world, she consists of the kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, and is mixed with the elements.
The body is said to be threefold; it is traditionally remembered as the gross, the subtle, and the supreme.
The gross is the body of the elements, while the subtle is the *puryaṣṭaka*. (19)
Furthermore, that which arises from the Bindu is declared to be threefold:
namely, the Āṇava, the Māyīya, and the Kārma—this constitutes the triad of impurities (malas).
The *āṇava* [impurity] is said to be like a husk and a bamboo sheath respectively;
the *sahaja* [impurity], however, is bound to the impurity and is described as being alone. (21)
One should know that this Māyā binds the individual soul (śaktikā), characterized by the levels beginning with Kalā down to the earth; it is born from karma known as merit and demerit.
This human action is illusory and has such a limited duration;
having seen that this action is of three kinds, some of which are to be experienced in the present life.
Through the power of perfected mantras, longevity, yoga, medicine, and so forth, yield their fruit in that very birth; one does not relinquish the enjoyment perceived therein. (24)

In the Śivadarśana, that karma which is to be experienced at the end of the body as waves of one's own sovereignty, and which is not perceived [until then], is called "adṛṣṭavedanīya" (to be experienced unseen). 25.

Likewise, it consists briefly of destiny and that which is to be experienced in time; and it is likewise classified as pertaining to the self (ādhyātmika), to the elements (ādhibhautika), and to the divine (ādhidaivika). || 26 ||
One encounters three kinds of suffering, whose distinctions are manifold;
unrighteousness (adharma) is to be understood through its divisions according to the various modifications of the mind. (27)
Coarse, subtle, and extremely subtle— divided in many ways by millions of distinctions—
it undergoes differentiation during dissolution and is employed for its creation. (28)
And at the end, one abides in Māyā; it is said that even the liberated is not destroyed.
Karma is threefold: that which has begun (prārabdha), that which is accumulated (sañcita), and that which is yet to come (āgāmi). || 29 ||
Desire, non-desire, and the desire of another—thus the *prārabdha* (commenced karma) becomes threefold;
it is pierced by the threefold sheath, gradually fashioned by Time. || 30 ||
Embraced by necessity (niyati), it proceeds through the path of the mind and the vital breath;
the time of creation, the time of maintenance, and the time of dissolution are thus considered to be threefold. (31)
They exist in three times; from that [sequence], the past and the future [arise].
(What is called the "present" time is stated separately.
When the completion of the remainder occurs, that is traditionally known as the "beginning. || 32 ||
That which is dependent on [other] factors at a given time is called "future" (anāgata);
that which has been commenced but is not yet completed is cited as "present" (vartamāna). || 33 ||
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are declared to be the three qualities (guṇas).
Right knowledge, austerity, silence, memory, intelligence, fortitude, and forbearance [are the manifestations of sattva]. || 34 ||
Enthusiasm, resolve, and long-suffering—these indeed are the qualities of the sattvic type;
while pride, great egoism, despondency, and pleasant speech [are otherwise]. (35)
Agitation and envy are declared to be the quality of passion (rājasa);
likewise, laziness, delusive sleep, and fickleness constitute the base conduct [of tamas]. (36)
The most wicked act of reviling others is said to be the quality of darkness (tāmasa);
yet, in its essential nature, it does not differ from the other qualities in reality. (37)
The equilibrium of the unmanifest qualities is recited as the Pradhāna;
however, the equilibrium of the differentiated qualities is here called the Guṇatattva.

The state of divinity arises from the *sāttvika* [nature], the human state indeed from the *rājasa*, and the state of being an animal one attains through the *tāmasa*; such is this threefold destiny. (39)
Sattva is the cause of action, while rajas is the cause of activity; tamas, however, consists of obscuration.
Ego (ahaṃkāra) is said to be threefold, characterized by the exertion and pride of the individual soul (jīva).
Agitation, egoism, manifestation, and the cognition of other objects—this is the supreme wind produced by the fivefold activity that impels life. (41)
One who holds a position common to the village deities does not desire conflict;
for what agent can be made of that which has been performed by me for the sake of the world? (42)
That very self, divided into its constituent parts, is called the limb of the knowledge of reality;
and it is declared to be threefold, the first of which pertains to fire.

The second is the vaikārika [ego], and the next is that which abounds in the elements (bhūtādhika); that which is characterized by the predominance of sattva is here called "by its own radiance" (svatejas).
The Vaikṛta [ego] is preeminent among the rājasa; the Bhūtādi is predominant in tamas. Because it is the origin of the elements (bhūtas), it is called Bhūtādi. || 45 ||

The Puruṣa is traditionally taught to exist in three states: the isolated (kevala), the all-pervasive (sakala), and the pure (śuddha). There is no doubt that the state of purity is the self (ātman) which is called Śiva. || 46 ||
Having known the three states and so forth, rebirth no longer exists;
[he is] the Lord because he is the impeller of insentient things such as Māyā. (47)
Siddhi is the accomplisher of all aims, the agent, all-pervading, and eternally blissful;
for the benefit of practitioners, it assumes a body by its own will.
That body should be known as threefold: the partless (niṣkala), that which consists of both, and the manifest (sakala);
thus, according to the scripture, it exists with these three divisions in sequence.
The Supreme is said to be partless (niṣkala), while the Lower is remembered as having parts (sakala). Likewise, the Higher-Lower is declared to be both with and without parts (sakala-niṣkala).
Having meditated upon the higher and the lower as they truly are, he becomes liberated and a destroyer of bonds;
for there exist three divisions in due order: dissolution, enjoyment, and authority. || 51 ||
The agent is held to be threefold according to the activity of the hundred [faculties]: capable, engaged, and active;
the distinction among these is merely figurative based on the difference in activity.
Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta are remembered as the three by name;
likewise, Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Maheśa are recorded as the triad. (53)

The power of the principles (tattva), the forms (mūrti), and [the mantras] exist in three divisions respectively; that which begins with Śiva is called the principle, while the forms begin with Sadāśiva. (54)
The form that arises from the union of those two is called Bhāva.
It is considered to be threefold: Hariṇī, Jananī, and Rodhayantrī. || 55 ||
The *hariṇī* posture, which has been described for Śiva and is adorned with all ornaments,
or else, having drawn in the *pudgala*, one should lead it to another position.

Because this power [śakti] arises from Him, she is called "the deer-colored one" (hariṇī) by the wise; she is the mother of the two worlds, the birth of her own nature, and the radiance of the primordial state. 57.
Because she likewise ordains that even for him, who is established in restraint during the dissolution of the world-restraining Saṅgha, there shall be enjoyment as well. 58.
These three powers, O brahmins, which consist of the body and the instruments [of action], are eternally established as the inherent strength of the omnipresent Lord. (59)
Will, knowledge, and action are declared to be the triad of powers;
through the power of knowledge one discerns, and through the power of action one creates the universe.
And when Śiva was devoid of compassion, all knowledge was then taken away;
thus, three powers are to be known as belonging to the cause, whose nature is imperishable.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī are declared to be the Śaktis;
through the immersion (samāveśa) of the Śakti Raudrī, [the manifestation] preceded by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others occurs.
(26) That knowledge which pervades all activities and by which it is accompanied by its own nature—
because of its possession of all knowledge, the Supreme Lord is omniscient. || 63 ||
The existence of an omniscient being is also established by scripture, due to the observation of the greatness of his qualities;
just as the sun causes the lotuses to bloom with its rays. (64)
It blossoms everywhere according to its own respective karma, because Prakṛti is insentient and Puruṣa is the sovereign. || 65 ||
The universe and its creator are considered to be entirely dependent upon parts;
likewise, Mahādeva, the Great Lord, is the creator of my very self and of the universe.

The one who binds and the act of binding are established as the three bonds themselves; through the expression of the relationship between the goal and the means, they become clearly manifest exactly as they are.
The sacrificial animals (paśus) are to be known as threefold according to the distinction between the higher and the lower:
Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Śānta; these are considered the supreme Gurus. (68)
May Anantaśrī, Śiva, Umā, Skanda, Viṣṇu, Svadhiti, Parāpara, Varedeva, the sages, and the three most excellent Gurus be pleased. (69)
Brahmā, Śiva, Ugrajyotis, Sadyojyotis, and Bṛhaspati— these five,
beginning with Ākaṇṭha, were the founders of the Śiva scriptures, extending from the feet up to the throat.
And others are those who dwell at the feet of their own guru, whether householders or celibate students;
namely, the impeller, the awakener, and the third, the giver of liberation. || 71 ||
One should worship all [deities] as if they were Śiva, because they grant liberation to human beings;
and she who impels knowledge toward Śiva, the supreme cause. (72)

They say that the one who impels is the "impeller" (preraka); the preceptor of initiation (dīkṣāguru) is the best among the sons of the Guru. But the one who grants liberation is the enlightener (bodhaka), the revealer of the scriptures. || 73 ||

Likewise, the awakener (bodhaka) must indeed be honored with effort, according to the distinctions such as the instigator (codaka) and so forth, just as [the distinctions] among teachers (guru) and others are made. || 74 ||
The Guru is the performer of initiation alone; the Deśika is the expounder;
and the Ācārya is the one who performs installations and so forth, as well as the instructor of other disciples. (75)
The Ācārya, the Sadguru, and the Svāmī—these are the three forms of the Guru.
The Ācārya is for the sake of training the novice, while the Sadguru is for the awakening to the Mantra. (76)
They provide instruction on liberation and are called "the Master.
In the Śiva-āgama, they are known as Śāmbhavī, Śāktī, and Mantreśī. (77)
Initiation is taught by Śiva, the Supreme Self, as being threefold:
through the mere glance of the Guru, through touch, and also through speech. (78)
Knowledge arises immediately; that is remembered as the Śāmbhavī initiation.
And the Śākta initiation, possessing the power of knowledge, enters the body of the disciple. (79)
By means of the path of yoga, the preceptor, possessing the eye of knowledge,
performs the initiatory rite consisting of mantra and ritual action, preceded by the sacrificial pit and the mandala.
Measurement (māna), standard measure (pramāṇa), and height measurement (unmāna) are proclaimed to be threefold.
Measurement is said to be length (āyāma), while standard measure (pramāṇa) constitutes the width (vistara). (81)
It is said that "I am not" is the measure of the Unmanifest; thus, the threefold measure has been illustrated.
The first is the finger-measure (mānāṅguli), and the second is the digit-measure (mātrāṅguli). 82.
The third finger-breadth obtained from the body is of three kinds:
the atom (paramāṇu), the lower unit (adhaḥ), and the tip of a louse's hair (piśukeśāgra). || 83 ||
A louse, a nit, and a barley grain increase eightfold in succession;
this is declared to be the *mānāṅgula*. Now hear about the *mātrāṅgula*.
In the middle joint of the middle finger of the teacher’s right hand, the circumference is said to be of three kinds: long, equal, and short. (85)
In the case of palaces, pavilions, and the like, as well as for walls and gate-towers (gopura),
and for villages, fields, and similar entities, the measurement shall be according to the rule of the *mānāṅgula*.

The vessels for the planets, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and so forth, must be made according to the measurement of finger-breadths (*mātrāṅgula*). One should not use another measurement; if one were to do so, it would be fruitless.
One should have images and other such objects fashioned using exactly the finger-breadths obtained from the body;
the measurement obtained from the body is threefold, according to the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior. (88)
The span formed by joining the thumb and the index finger is known as a *prādeśa*;
that formed by joining the thumb and the ring finger is called a *vidhasti*. (89)
The joining of the little finger and the thumb is known as *gokarṇa*.
These three—the *prādeśa*, the *vidhasta*, and the *gokarṇa*—are [the measures]. (90)
It should be employed in sacrifices and similar rites, but one should not cause it to be given for temples and such;
when the middle finger is joined with the thumb, that is called a *tāla*.

A wise person should employ the measurement of *tāla* units when constructing temples and similar edifices; likewise, one should divide the height of an image according to the calculation of *tāla* units. (92)
The best [type] consists of one hundred and twenty-four *daśatāla*s;
the middling is one hundred and twenty, while the smallest begins at sixteen.
Up to one hundred and twelve *tālas* it shall be the best;
likewise, eight hundred and four hundred [tālas] are the middling and the smallest respectively.
One hundred and ninety-six, and two more with nine added;
this is declared to be the eight-fold tāla, which, as before, is of three kinds.
Thus, it should be diminished by one part until it ends at one tāla;
this threefold [measurement] in ten tālas is proclaimed for the three deities.
The height of the wives of the gods is three times nine tālas;
that of mortals is eight tālas, and that of the Rākṣasas is seven tālas.
The Gandharvas should be six tālas, the Lord of the Gaṇas five tālas;
likewise, Vāmana should be [five], while the Bhūtas should be four tālas.
For the Kinnaras it is three tālas; for the Yakṣas, two tālas;
and likewise for those born from eggs, specifically for the Piśācas, one tāla. (99)
A devotee should construct a collection of temples according to his means;
whether small or large, the fruit is equal for both the wealthy and the poor.
Therefore, one-third of one's wealth should be set aside for one's own livelihood, and two parts for the sake of dharma, for life is indeed eternal. (101)
Even a man of little wealth who performs [the rite] with devotion according to his means, yet acts with deceit regarding his wealth or with deceit regarding the dharma, [is as follows]. (102)
One whose mind is overcome by greed does not obtain the fruit of that [action].
The temple is said to be of three kinds, distinguished as Nāgara and so forth. (103)
It is considered to be of three kinds: Nāgara, Drāviḍa, and Vesara.
That which is circular starting from the neck is known as Vesara. (104)
Starting from the neck, the octagonal vimāna is called Drāviḍa;
whereas that which is entirely square is this Nāgara temple.
Now, the three types of temples according to the measurement of the *liṅga* will be described:
in the Nāgara style, the *liṅga* is Nāgara, and likewise in the Vesara style, it is Vesara.
The Liṅga is declared to be of three types: Nāgara, Drāviḍa, and indeed Veśara.
The Nāgara is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa, while the Drāviḍa is for the Kṣatriya.
The *vesara* is known in the *Smṛti* as the mixed caste (*jātibheda*) of Vaiśyas and Śūdras;
Īśa, Pitāmaha, and Viṣṇu are the presiding deities (*adhidaivata*) therein. (108)
The Nāgara is the masculine temple, the Drāviḍa is the feminine, and the Vesara is the neuter; thus the temple is said to be of three kinds. (109)
It is declared that the posture established on the feet is the *pratibandha* (obstructive) posture;
make the *prāsādaka* (gracious) posture of the present *liṅga* firm. 110.
The *liṅga* established on its pedestal should have a squatting posture (*pratibandhāsana*).
For those *liṅgas* that exceed the measurement of Śiva, one should cause it to be made in a seated posture (*āsīna*) there.
The reclining posture of the Trairāśika Liṅga is called Prāsāda;
it is taught that when one foot is firmly planted, it becomes Pratibandhāsana. || 112 ||
The *padmabandha* posture for reclining is to be known through the various arrangements of the feet; likewise, there are the *ārṣaka*, *sthānaka*, *svāyaṃbhuva*, and *ārhatam* postures. (113)
The human [type] consists of arrows, the Rākṣasa of beds, and the Gāṇava of couches;
the Daivika is said to consist of vehicles—such are the characteristics described.
A liṅga situated upon a square pedestal is said here to be "standing" (sthita); one that is perfectly circular is declared to be "mental" (mānasa), and an octagonal one is "reclining" (śayana).
That which is made from a single substance is pure; that which is fashioned from two substances is mixed;
and that which is fashioned from three substances is proclaimed to be "contaminated" (saṅkīrṇa). || 116 ||
(32) The manifestation of the abode in the worlds of Svāyambhuva and others occurs through a single substance;
at the time of its decay, one should firmly bind that very same substance. 117.
If it is made from other materials, the king and the kingdom perish. [The parts are:
the head-dome (śirasthūpī), the neck (gala), the neck-ornament (mañja), the base (pādādhiṣṭhāna), and the cloth (aṃśaka). 118.

The *upāṅga* consists of the *kūṭa* and *śāla*, while the *pratyaṅga* is the nose and the five-fold lattice; that which extends from the golden base (*hemādi*) to the pinnacle (*sthūpī*) is known as the *sthūlaliṅga*.
The gross liṅga is the vimāna, the subtle liṅga is Sadāśiva, and the auspicious liṅga is the pedestal for offerings; thus the triad of liṅgas is proclaimed.
The body is said to be the temple, and the embodied soul is remembered as the linga; there is no difference between the two, therefore one should contemplate them in this way. 121.
Alternatively, the best of teachers should meditate upon Sadāśiva as the gross liṅga and Śiva as the internal liṅga.
The pervasive [deity] alone, in the form of pervasion, is the means of measurement;
whatever rite is performed without that measurement shall be fruitless. || 123 ||
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the installation of the celestial chariot (vimāna),
as well as the prescribed rites for the palace, the pavilion, and the gateway.

Establish the enclosure wall and other structures according to the [prescribed] signs; likewise, there are the self-manifested (svāyaṃbhuva), the stone (bāṇa), the divine (daivika), and the sage-made (ārṣaka) liṅgas.
Furthermore, regarding that which was established by the great-souled ones as a perfected Vidyādhara,
the wise man should construct a temple according to their respective lingas. (126)
Therefore, I shall describe the temple of Pauruṣaliṅga;
once that has been established in the east, even if the original temple was previously unknown.
One should design the temple strictly according to the measurement of the *liṅga*.
It is said that the *liṅga* is of three kinds: manifest (*vyakta*), unmanifest (*avyakta*), and of the nature of both. (128)
That which is manifest (vyakta) is considered to be with parts (sakala), while that which is unmanifest (avyakta) is regarded as partless (niṣkala).
The Liṅga consisting of the light of knowledge is remembered as both manifest and unmanifest (vyaktāvyakta). || 129 ||
It is of three kinds: moving, moving-and-unmoving, and unmoving.
The moving [liṅga] is to be worshipped in one's own self; the bāṇaliṅga is the moving-and-unmoving. || 130 ||
Among those, the gate-towers (gopura) and so forth that are immovable are praised;
however, the shaking of the head of Ananta is said to be the wrath of the Fire of Time (Kālāgni).
From his anger, sparks [emerged], and thus the Svāyambhuva [Purāṇa] became threefold;
it is remembered as being "without root," "with root," and "well-prefaced" (supūrva). || 132 ||
That which is rootless is submerged in water, while that which has roots rests upon mountains;
the word of a reliable authority (āptavākya) is of three kinds, beginning with that which is "well-preceded" (supūrva), namely the Svāyambhuva [Purāṇa]. 133.
Endowed with various marks and possessed of various colors, it is invariably seen on earth as being hard and characterized by cavities and the like. (134)
(34) It is proclaimed in exactly this same way regarding all the *nāgas* as well:
likewise, there is the rubbing of the head and the rolling of the thread. (135)
Neither an excess nor a deficiency is ever observed;
however, the pedestal and the temple-like structure are fashioned according to the measurement of the *liṅga*.
That which is called "self-manifested" (svayambhūta) brings happiness to all the worlds;
however, one should not clean the root-linga that constitutes the visible lower portion.
If one digs up a Rudra [image] out of delusion or ignorance and gazes upon it, he destroys the food of the king and the makers of the village-dwellers. (138)
Therefore, one should not look at the root; rather, act according to the preceding portion.
It is threefold: Citra, Citrārdhaka, and Citrābhāsa. (139)
A painting in which all the limbs are complete is called "visible" (dṛśya);
that in which half the limbs are visible is here called "half-visible" (madhyacitra). || 140 ||
When the letter *dha* is written on the foot or the wall, it is known as *citrābhāsa*.
O Vanānala of beautiful speech, listen as I shall now fully describe the *āsana*. 141.

Indeed, the "unbroken" (akhaṇḍa) and the "broken" (khaṇḍa) tips are said to be of three kinds; that which extends from the netherworld (pātāla) to the highest realm (parānta) is praised as the unbroken. || 142 ||
That which begins with Vasudā and ends with Vanā is known as this Khaṇḍa;
that which begins with Śakti and ends with Śiva is celebrated as Tuṇḍa.

In the case of an unbroken, partless [liṅga], it should be conceived as being without a *tuṇḍa*; however, in the case of a broken [liṅga] or a *bimba*, one should likewise fashion a *tuṇḍa* for a momentary or mobile liṅga. (144)
A Liṅga that has been established should be unbroken; however, an image may be broken. Wall-paintings and the like, as well as the Tuṇḍaliṅga, are also highly praised. || 145 ||

Having recited all the mantras— whether whispered (upāṃśu), spoken aloud (vācika), or mentally (mānasa)— it is declared that the whispered method applies to the sacrifice, while the spoken method applies to the act of oblation (homa).
In the recitation of mantras, the mental [recitation] is declared to be the best among all mantras.
Sacrifice is said to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior. (147)
Worship performed solely with Śiva-mantras shall be the most excellent;
worship performed with both Vedic and Śiva-mantras shall be middling. || 148 ||
Sacrificing solely with Vedic mantras would be inferior;
therefore, for one's own benefit, one should perform sacrifice with Śaiva mantras, which is supreme. (149)
Worship may be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
That which is performed solely with mantras declared in the pure Śaiva tradition is called superior. (150)
The middle [level] is indeed by means of the meanings of the Vedas, while the lowest is considered to be by means of Vedic [mantras].
There is no mantra equal to the Śaiva mantra in the three worlds. 151.
In that regard, the root mantra is said to be the most excellent, being the essence of the seed-syllable.
The fire-ritual (agnikārya) is considered to be threefold: Vedic, mixed, and Śaiva. || 152 ||
(36) One who is initiated solely by means of prescribed Vedic mantras becomes a Vaidika;
one who is initiated by both Vedic and Śaiva mantras is called Miśra (Mixed). || 153 ||
That which is performed solely with Śiva-mantras is called Śaiva;
for Brāhmaṇas it is Vaidika, while for kings it is Vaidikatantrika.
For Vaiśyas and Śūdras, the mantra is indeed Tantric, or for all [castes], it may be Tantric;
the mantra should be known as threefold: the garland-mantra, the seed-syllable, and the sequential phrase. 155.
The form of mantra is threefold: pure, mixed, and composite.
A pure mantra consists of a single syllable; a mixed mantra may also consist of a single syllable. || 156 ||
The mixed mantra has many forms, yet it becomes threefold;
the wise know its measures (mātrās) to be one, two, and three, respectively, as short, long, and protracted.
That which consists of one measure is short; that which consists of two measures is called long;
that which consists of three measures is to be known as protracted (pluta); and a consonant is half a measure. || 158 ||

The short [vowel] is situated in the bindu, the long in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and the protracted (pluta) is conjoined with the limit of the twelve; this is the Prāsāda mantra for the purification of the mantra. 159.
The short [form] burns away sins; the long [form] becomes the bestower of liberation;
and the prolated [form], adorned with a *bindu* at the crown, becomes nourished. 160.
The three gross bodies are prescribed for subjugation (vaśya), eradication (uccāṭana), and killing (māraṇa);
indeed, the *pluta* [breath-retention] always effects subjugation—of this there is no doubt. (161)
The long [vowel], when joined with the six-syllable [mantra], swiftly causes expulsion;
likewise, the six-syllable [mantra] placed at the beginning or the end of the short [vowel] is beneficial for killing. (162)
It is proclaimed that it draws the heart toward itself at both the beginning and the end;
O Six-faced One, the short vowel is said to belong to the Brāhmaṇī class, while the long vowels are its limbs.
The mantra should have the *anusvāra* situated above all [its syllables];
having understood it as gross, subtle, and supreme, one may perform the ritual action as desired. (164)
The gross is said to consist of sound, while the subtle consists of thought;
that which is accompanied by thought is proclaimed as the supreme.
The Prāsāda has been described by me as being gross, subtle, and supreme;
by that through which they understand the Prāsāda, they understand Śaṅkara.
He who knows the temple as the great body of the five mantras, endowed with the thirty-eight kalās, is not called an ācārya. (167)
If a guru performs initiation without correctly understanding the temple (prāsāda), he burns neither the disciple nor himself; of this there is no doubt. (168)
Indeed, the preceptor who bestows initiation while remaining within the temple-lotus of Śiva shall attain union with Śiva, together with his disciples. || 169 ||
All ritual actions, such as plowing and so forth, are declared to be performed by means of mantra alone;
therefore, because the purpose of ritual action is the mantra, there is indeed no ritual action apart from the mantra.
The deity is to be installed with a mantra; the sacrifices and other rites are performed with a mantra;
bathing and sipping water are done with mantras; and the oblation and the libation are offered with a mantra. (171)
Indeed, by means of the *prāyaścitta* mantra and the initiation (*dīkṣā*) mantra,
as well as by the mantra, powers such as *aṇimā* and states such as *sālokya* may come to be.
By means of the mantra, one is freed from all evils, beginning with the soles of the feet;
it is a source of honor because of its omniscience, and a protection from the ocean of saṃsāra. (173)
It is called "mantra" because it has the nature of honoring and protecting;
it is of three kinds: pure, mixed, and for one's own benefit. || 174 ||
Whether it be pure and devoid of power, or solitary and conjoined with power—from Saura up to Caṇḍa—if it is mixed, it is proclaimed as such. (175)
In some cases, worship is of three kinds: solitary, innate, and mixed.
Solitary worship involves a single *liṅga*, while innate worship involves five images (*bera*).
The combined [installation] of the images of Maheśvara and the others is called "mixed" (miśra). Likewise, the images of Gaṇeśa, Skanda, Śakti, and the Bull [are included]. (177)
That which is joined with the *liṅga* alone is proclaimed as "Sahaja" (the Innate);
and that which is joined with the Sahaja is Maheśa, whose form is the Dance. (178)
Those images which are for the sake of desired objects are called "mixed" (sahita) or "combined" (miśra).
One should worship the Śaiva image that is pure and alone, having been honored by one who has conquered the senses. 179.
The teacher should worship both the Miśraka and the Kevala Śuddha [forms].
This should always be performed with effort by those desiring spiritual success (*siddhi*) in the case of a fixed linga. (180)
Worship of Śiva at a mobile liṅga bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men;
it is considered to be of three kinds: pure, mixed, and common, when performed for the sake of others. (181)

The pure [form of worship] ends with the offering of oblations (havis), the mixed ends with the daily festival (nityotsava), and the impure ends with the pure dance (śuddhanṛtta); thus, worship is said to be of three kinds. || 182 ||
The worship that is performed by people in the morning, at midday, and in the evening—whether it be pure, mixed, or especially confused—one should perform it with care. (183)
Whether on the road to prosperity or during all the twilight periods, in every way,
the attainment of mixed or confused [states] is not desired by one who knows that.
That twilight itself shall be the worship; such is the certainty of the scripture.
Worship is of three kinds: pure, mixed, and impure. || 185 ||
The pure *svāyaṃbhuva* linga, the mixed *mānuṣaka*, and the combined [linga] of the five forms (*pañcamūrti*) for the sake of others—these are considered the threefold [classification]. (186)

He [taught] that worship of the local deity leads to liberation, worship of Viṣṇu for the sake of wealth, and worship of Durgā for the sake of victory over enemies; and specifically, it bestows the desire for a son.
The granting of desired boons and the worship of Skanda result from the adoration of the five images;
a wise person should perform worship for their own sake according to their capacity and inclination. (188)
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, [the ritual] ends with the lamp and the sacrificial offering (havis).
Worship is said to end with the lamp, while the act of honoring (pūjana) ends with the food offering (naivedya). (189)

The *śāntika* rite is said to end with the offering of oblations (*bali*), and worship (*pūjā*) may be of three kinds: that which ends with the lamp and water is for *sāvaśya*, while that which ends with the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is for *saubhāgya*. (190)
It should be gentle and conclude with a constant festival; worship is of three kinds.
Worship is said to end with the lamp-offering, and its fruit is indeed the triad of the "lesser" (kanyasa) levels.
The seed-mantra (bīja) is said to conclude with the fire-oblation (homa); the propitiatory rite (śāntika) concludes with the festival (utsava);
and the nourishing rite (pauṣṭika) is said to conclude with the hymn of praise (stotra). Indeed, these three constitute the lowest grade of results.

There shall be happiness and an increase in liberation; it brings prosperity up to the end of the *culuka* [the hollowed palm]; it makes the *prāṇāgnihotra* fruitful, and its fruit is indeed ninefold. (193)
The three lowest [levels] end with the lamp, the offering, and the bali;
the three middle [levels] end with the fire-oblation, the festival, and the hymn of praise.
The "Fistful of Water" (Culakodānta) rite for happiness, and the "Life-Force Fire-Sacrifice" (Prāṇāgnihotra)—
these are declared to be the three supreme [practices], which bestow the fruit of worship and great supernatural power.
The experts in dance have declared that there are three varieties of dance: the pure, the grotesque, and likewise the highly expressive. || 196 ||
At the conclusion of the worship, a pure dance endowed with all auspicious characteristics should be performed by a daughter of Rudra, and never by anyone else.
The first is the sprout of the banner, the second is the sprout of the festival;
the third is the sprout of the sacred ford, and the fourth is the sprout of the festival. (198)
The first and the second are called the sprout of auspiciousness (maṅgalāṅkura);
the third shall be the limb of the festival (utsavāṅga). Thus, the sprout is of three kinds. || 199 ||
The festival is declared to be of three kinds: that preceded by the hoisting of the banner, that preceded by the beating of the drum, and that preceded by the sowing of seeds. || 200 ||
The festival preceded by the hoisting of the banner should take place on the third day;
however, that preceded by the beating of the drum is considered to occur on the second day. (201)
The rite beginning with the offering of the sprouts is prescribed for nine days;
however, O Guha, at the time of commencing the festival of Śiva, another festival is not desired.
If at the time of a festival for another deity, one performs a festival for Mahādeva,
he does not incur any fault, provided the festivals for other deities were previously commenced.
During that festival of Śiva, one who has begun [the rite] in the midst of it incurs all defects, if the worship of Śiva’s limbs and another sacrifice are performed at the same time. || 204 ||
One obtains that festival at a single site in vain;
no other banner should be made, but rather the bull-banner (Vṛṣabhadhvaja) should be made.
At a time auspicious for the gods, one should not perform an auspicious rite for humans;
if one should perform it out of delusion, there will be fear of disease and illness. (206)
It is threefold: obligatory, occasional, and optional. That which is to be performed every day is here called "obligatory" (nitya). (207)
Rituals such as the bathing festival and rites for pacification are considered occasional (naimittika); likewise, initiation and consecration would also be of this occasional nature. (208)
For the sake of attaining powers such as *aṇimā* and others, there may be optional rites (*kāmya*) for Vaiśyas and other castes.
These optional rites are to be understood as the means to attain the supernatural powers (*siddhi*), which are recorded as being of many kinds. (209)
The lowest is kingship and you [attain] the middling, which is the success of Bali;
the highest is the state of a Khecarī, equal to the most excellent gods. || 210 ||
Each one of these exists in many ways according to its distinctions, such as the state of a Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa) and so forth;
namely, the state of a Lord of Knowledge, the state of Rudra, the state of Brahmā, and the station of Viṣṇu.

One should know that the happiness which exists in the lower realms, such as Amareśa and other abodes of Rudra within the sphere of conditioned effects (kārya), is inferior; whereas the happiness of one established in the station of Ananta and others is supreme.
Bathing is considered to be of three kinds: obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya).
One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites out of a desire to avoid transgression.
One should not perform prohibited rites for the sake of desired objects;
when a doubt arises as to whether something ought to be done or ought not to be done— [214]
In the matter of ritual performance, prosperity is to be known as arising from correct action, while fault is said to arise from incorrect action;
therefore, that which is declared in the Śaiva scriptures must be performed, and not that which comes from other scriptures. (215)
If that which is prescribed there is not commended, one should then resort to another treatise;
and when that [other treatise] is also untenable, then the supplementary rule (pṛṣṭha-vidhi) is enjoined therein.
When penances and such are not mentioned in one's own scripture, they are to be taken from another scripture;
however, when the purpose of the scripture is already present, the implements such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are its constituent parts.
Whether it be established in one's own scripture or proclaimed in another scripture—having considered such matters as these, those best of kings should cause [the temple] to be built. (218)
In a short time, he shall conquer all sovereigns;
moreover, his lifespan and health shall be exactly as conceived by his mind. (219)
Everything belongs to him, and devotion to Śiva arises within him;
even upon seeing contrary actions, he maintains equanimity. || 220 ||
That king meets with ruin; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Therefore, O Teacher, it is proper that he should abide by the path of the five spheres of perception.

One who possesses the limbs of Śiva through supreme discernment and is engaged in ritual action should conduct his activities according to human conduct for the sake of the prosperity of his own kingdom. (222)
One who is proficient in the Śiva scriptures should receive [the teachings] from a guru who is even greater than a guru;
by that very person, the best of sages should cause the bathing and other rites to be performed.
The threefold rites—daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya)—have been prescribed for the teacher;
the preceptor must also perform these three, except for the installation of an image, when he has no son.

(44) The triad beginning with the daily rite (nitya) is to be performed as an exposition by the teacher; O Six-faced One, the daily and optional rites for the practitioner are those declared in his own scripture. (225)
For both the initiate (samayin) and the spiritual son (putraka), this is always proclaimed;
for that distinguished one, the daily rite (āhnika) consists of two parts joined with the morning twilight (prāksandhyā).
For one who has been initiated here, Nirvāṇa is declared to occur during the three junctions of the day;
for the Ācārya, however, it is specifically prescribed at midnight.
The supreme, the supreme-and-non-supreme, and the non-supreme are considered the threefold [division];
yet in reality, there is only one, the stainless supreme power of Śiva. (228)
Inseparable from Śambhu, she is the coolness of the pure Lord who is united with heat;
through her, she is the union of the Self and Śiva, the supreme and non-supreme consciousness of Śiva. (229)
This very twilight has been described, and it is further considered to be threefold;
those powers known as Kriyā, Dṛk, and Icchā exist upon the path of purity.
Together with those powers of the Śivas known as Ātma and Sva,
that twilight (saṃdhyā) is the beloved of the power Śamanā, ending with Bindu and Nāda.
These three junctions (saṃdhyās), which are higher than the highest, have been declared according to one's karma;
they should be meditated upon by those initiated into Nirvāṇa at the heart, the forehead, and the crown of the head.
That which is designated as Parā is called Turyā, the ender of the world;
she is endowed with the three qualities (guṇas) and is likewise Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Śāṅkarī. || 233 ||
(45) And these three powers are to be known by the wise as the three junctions (saṃdhyā);
they are indeed declared to be equal by the sons [of the Lord]. || 234 ||
These are to be meditated upon in sequence at the heart, the bindu, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Thus, they are the junctions (saṃdhyās) and the witnesses of all actions, including Caṇḍa.
The three qualities (guṇas) are indeed the highest, the middle, and the lowest;
likewise the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, and Maruts. || 236 ||
The Viśvedevas, the fathers and mothers, the planetary deities, Aṅgiras, the Aśvins, the gods, and likewise the hosts of the three deities; || 237 ||
In this world, the constellations, the [planets], and the providers of fortnights, as well as the lords of the principles (tattvas), are proclaimed to be the most excellent. || 238 ||
And the Siddhas, Yakṣas, Nāgas, Asuras, and even Rākṣasas; as well as the Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, and likewise the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis). || 239 ||
And the mortal beings of Rohiṇī are recorded as the middle group;
likewise, the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and kuśmāṇḍas are the first [group].
The Skandabālagraha, the terrifying Traihala, the Kinnaras, the Vetālas, the Apasmāra-grahas, and so forth. || 241 ||
Yoginī, Ḍākinī, Śākinī, Kālikā, and Lihinī—these are proclaimed to be the lowest among all [the classes]. (242)
The supreme and the middling [deities] are assigned among the retinues;
Rudrālayī is declared [to be the foremost], and they are celebrated among the retinues. (243)

The threefold ritual bathing is known as peaceful (śānti), gentle (saumya), and fierce (raudra). For the sake of prosperity, the water for the jar is prescribed to be three finger-breadths deep at the feet.
The tip of that uneven foot is considered to be nine finger-breadths;
from the middle of those two sides, the division should be thoroughly understood.

The *ṛju* (straight) posture is known as the *vaiśākha* stance; the *saumya* (gentle) is with the left leg extended, while the *raudra* (fierce) is known by the reverse of that. The characteristics of these two [postures] are the same.
Among those, the first is said to bestow liberation; the second bestows both enjoyment and liberation.
The fierce [state] is the cessation of passions, as shown by the path of the stations. (247)
Bliss is to be known as threefold:
the supreme, the non-supreme, and likewise that which is even higher than the supreme; thus it is proclaimed to be threefold. (248)
The Vāma and Dakṣiṇa Siddhāntas constitute the threefold Śuddhaśaiva;
these are the root and derivative Tantras, which form the scripture known as Vāmaśaiva. (249)
The scriptures such as the *Svacchanda* and others are called the Southern Śaiva;
the tantras such as the *Kāmika* and others are called the Siddhānta Śaiva. || 250 ||
Likewise, there are seven case-endings (vibhakti), each of which is considered to be threefold;
they are to be employed in sequence according to the numbers one, two, and many. (251)
The masculine, the feminine, and the neuter as the third—these are the genders. The nominative case is prescribed for the mere expression of gender, as well as for addressing. (252)

One should employ the remaining [suffixes] according to the action (karman) in the sense of the principal object; likewise, those beneficial [suffixes] are used in the sense of the point of departure (apādāna), the relationship (saṃbandha), and the agent (nirdhartṛ). || 253 ||
Having understood the connection of the meaning, one should employ the locative case for the object;
the locative may be employed in the sense of the genitive, and conversely, the genitive in the sense of the locative. (254)
By this sequential method, one should conduct legal proceedings;
the seven factors (kārakas) should be applied to the actions (karmas) according to the requirements of the case. 255.

One who always recites [the text] in this manner—relying on what has been heard and what has been inferred—should provide an explanation with diligent effort, remaining concentrated on both the word and the sentence. (256)
In this world, when speech proceeds devoid of its true meaning, it should be known as an *apaśabda* (corrupt word), whether it be in Sanskrit or even in Prākṛt. (257)
The wise understand that the seven *gamakas*—*ṛṣika*, *devabhāṣita*, and so forth—as well as the *āgamas* and *apaśabdas*, describe [the nature of] sounds. (258)
By means of this corrupted [speech], which is soft and charming, consisting of words of ignorance and passion, and serving as the cause for the afflictions of saṃsāra; || 259 ||
That speech which, upon being heard, generates merit and the complete destruction of sins and other evils, should be known as particularly distinguished and exceedingly beautiful. (260)
The first, the middle, and the supreme—thus the person is threefold;
the wise know each of these through the application of the three voices. (261)

When employing personal pronouns, the first person is used; thereafter, the second person begins with the pair [of endings]; but when the word "we" (asmad) is used, one should apply the third person at the beginning of the verbal root. 262.

One should indicate here the application of the nominal stem (*pratipadika*) according to its meaning, including the *karṇika* and the vicinity of the *vasphuṭa*, as well as the usage of the present tense and other tenses in their respective functions. (263)
The designation of the middle voice (ātmanepada), the active voice (parasmaipada), and both;
as well as consonants, vowels, euphonic combinations (saṃdhi), and case endings (vibhakti). || 264 ||
Nouns, verbs, prefixes, and likewise secondary derivatives (taddhita) constitute the parts; through various suffixes, the root is intended to express manifold meanings. (265)

The binding of feet (pādabandha) should be composed, while the prose composition (vṛttabandha) is called cūrṇikā; those expert in the science of grammar should understand this as a word ending in a case inflection.
That which is joined with persistent syllables and endowed with word-segments—such a word should be known as "persistent" (nirbandha), which is authoritative and of a fixed nature. || 267 ||
In this [treatise], there are twenty-six sections by number;
these are the *pādachandas*, consisting of the even (*sama*), the half-even (*ardhasama*), and likewise the uneven (*viṣama*). || 268 ||
In brief, a meter joined with *chandas* is held to be of three kinds;
that which has four quarters characterized by identical metrical marks [is one type]. (269)
Those who know the principles of the science of prosody declare that to be *samavṛtta* (even meter),
wherein the third foot is identical to the first foot. (270)

The third [type], however, is called *samayavadvṛtta* (even-yava-measure) when it possesses four quarters that are identical to one another, yet distinct from each other in their defining characteristics (*lakṣma*). (271)
Regarding this, those expert in the science of prosody say that it is an uneven meter (viṣamavṛtta),
characterized by an excessive number of word-breaks in its construction and an indefinite number of syllables.
The wise one should know that the syllable and word depend on the meaning, and the word is like a grain of powder to be known;
it is established as being of three kinds: verse, prose, and mixed. || 273 ||
Verse consists of four lines, and that is of two kinds: *vṛtta* (metre) and *jāti* (class).
Having understood the composition of word-strings without [fixed] feet, the poet creates it. (274)
Speech consisting of both prose and verse is called *campū*.
Poetry is classified as feminine, masculine, and neuter; their distinctions have thus been illustrated. (275)
Having recognized that masculine poetry is praiseworthy, the middling is charming, and the neuter is indeed inferior, the poet composes accordingly. (276)
The mind is to be known as masculine; fear and the remover of fear are feminine;
all other groups are proclaimed to be neuter. || 277 ||
Furthermore, perception may be of three kinds: dependent on the sense organs, independent [of them], and likewise dependent on the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). || 278 ||
In that state, independent of the senses and having completely abandoned all bonds,
