the union of the power of consciousness with all phenomena is considered the supreme yoga. (279)
Or rather, it would depend upon the sense-faculties for the sake of warding off injury;
through the power of dependence on the sense-faculties, there is the perception of objects by means of them. (280)
The connection of the power of consciousness with the object of meditation is dependent upon the internal organ;
this is established through both positive and negative concomitance, as well as by the method of pure negative concomitance.
These—namely, the purely positive and so forth—are observed in sequence as:
[the reason] being a property of the subject, absent from the similar instances (sapakṣa), and excluded from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa). || 282 ||
The negative instance (apāya) is its counter-correlative, consisting of the method of difference and the method of agreement;
the subject (pakṣa) is endowed with the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), while the similar instance (sapakṣa) is endowed with the same property.
That which possesses the same properties as that [subject] would be the counter-example (vipakṣa), arising from another thing being established. [Examples of fallacies are:
"being a woman" as the connection with twilight, "having a female form" as a ghost, and "counter-balanced opposition" (satpratipakṣatā). || 284 ||
The reason that follows from the absence of the probandum is one [type], while the other is likewise devoid of similar instances (sapakṣa).
Its illustration is: "Because it is different from smoke, like a taste-possessor. (285)
Let the world, presided over by Kopa, be understood as the non-duality of the effect;
know that there are three kinds of ascetics: the *tapasvin*, the *vivarnya*, and likewise [the *yati*]. (286)
The "learned" (vidvān) are said to be of three kinds; their characteristics are now described.
Those devoted to austerity are called ascetics (tapasvin); their conduct is restrained.
One should never study [this], nor form intentions regarding it, nor listen to it; likewise, one should neither gather disciples nor reveal this knowledge. (288)
He should not speak in refined Sanskrit, nor carry a staff or a water-pot;
having honored the external mark only momentarily, he should remain endowed with mere devotion. (289)
Alone at the foot of a tree, or observing silence or abstaining from it, he should dwell free from fear of others, using his own arm as a pillow. || 290 ||
He may wear whatever clothing he obtains, and likewise eat and drink from whatever vessel; his livelihood consists of food obtained by begging, whether held in his hands or in a bowl.
Thus addressed, O Nandikeśvara, a practitioner who is a human ascetic should become an ascetic; such is the conduct for both the learned man and the ascetic. (292)
Teaching, studying, listening, and reflecting—these four are especially [prescribed] for that wise man. (293)

There is a distinction between the learned and the striving; the former consists of exposition and reflection, while the latter, characterized by the "emerging" [state], does not exist without the consecration of a true teacher. (294)
For ascetics in the four stages of life (āśrama), three types [of conduct] are to be known among the Śaivas;
although there is a distinction between the stages of life, no distinction exists in their ultimate goal (niṣṭhā). || 295 ||
One who maintains both for the sake of liberation enjoys the fruit of both. (295½)
Thus ends the third chapter.
52) || Now follows the Chapter on Meaning (Arthavarga).
For in all the scriptures, the objects to be known are fourfold, namely:
the bound soul (paśu), the bond (pāśa), the Lord (pati), and Śiva, in that order. || 1 ||

The individual soul (paśu) is independent and consists of pure consciousness, yet it is defiled by impurity; it is deluded, eternally subject to transmigratory existence, possessing limited knowledge, lacking sovereignty, and devoid of action. (2)
The qualities (guṇas) are known as the noose (pāśa), while the two principles (dharmas) are known as impurity (mala).
They are innate to all living beings and exist like the tawny color and the blackness in copper.
The Lord Sadāśiva, who is the master of the mantras, whose essence is mantra and whose body is mantra, should be known as the manifestor of those [mantras] according to one's karma. || 4 ||
May that supreme Śiva be auspicious, who transcends mantra and is stainless;
[the four levels of speech are] Vaikharī, Madhyamā, another called Paśyantī, and the one known as Sūkṣmā.
Vaikharī is the object of the ear and is conceptual; Madhyamā is non-conceptual; the third is [Pashyantī]; the first is the instrument, and the last is the effect.
The instrument of Vaikharī is Madhyamā; Paśyantī is the instrument with respect to Madhyamā;
and Sūkṣmā, which is free from conceptual construction and consists of its own essential nature, is the instrument of Paśyantī.
The measures (*mātrā*) of the vital breaths (*vṛtti*) are fourfold and consist of the causal conditions (*pratyaya*).
Three are situated within, while the other is established externally. (8)

The subtle sound (nāda) becomes the drop (bindu); Paśyantī is the intermediate syllable. This fourfold [group] consists of resonance (saṅghoṣa), the resonance-less (ghoṣarahita), and that which agitates the drop (bindukṣobha).
Mātṛkā is to be known as Vaikharī; Suśivā and the others are the source of Nāda and the rest.
This very [power] has fourfold functions and is the substratum of the kalās, such as Nivṛtti and the others.
Furthermore, it is divided fivefold as the functions of the *kalā*s and so forth;
the four Vedas—*Ṛg*, *Yajus*, *Sāman*, and *Atharvan*—are thus proclaimed. (11)
The Mīmāṃsā, the Nyāya-śāstra, as well as the Purāṇas and the Smṛtis—these four are indeed the secondary limbs (upāṅgas), which are external limbs (bahiraṅgas). 12.
Āyurveda, Arthaveda, Dhanurveda, and likewise Gāndharvaveda—thus the Upavedas are of four kinds. || 13 ||
Mīmāṃsā is that which sets forth the meaning of all the Vedas for the sake of human goals, according to the divisions of dharma and adharma in accordance with the exertion of dharma. || 14 ||
The Dharmaśāstra is to be practiced as the regulator of duties;
it reveals longevity and health through its sections on causes, symptoms, and medicinal remedies.
Āyurveda is indeed the practice by which all subsist;
Arthaveda consists of food, drink, and so forth, for it is primarily devoted to that. (16)

(54) O Four-faced One, through the performance of the sacrificial fees, clarified butter, sacrificial cakes, and the preparation of the *caru* oblation, and by means of their preservation, this [rite] bestows the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*). 17.
In that context, the science of archery (Dhanurveda) serves to repel those who surround one;
for the application of the seven musical notes belongs to the Sāmaveda and the Gandharva-veda. (18)
Indeed, they proclaim each of the Upāṅgas and Upavedas:
the Buddhist, the Ārhata, the Pāñcarātra, and the Śaiva. (19)
The *samaya* (vow) may be of four kinds, yet its various divisions are manifold;
the scripture (*śāstra*) should be known as fourfold: Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, Miśra, and [Kaula]. (20)
Thus, the fourth [initiation] is proclaimed as being endowed with the Siddhānta;
those who have undergone initiation in due order according to the various scriptures, such as the Vāma and others, [attain this].
It is proclaimed as the Left (Vāmī), the Right (Dakṣiṇī), the Mixed (Miśrī), and the Established Doctrine (Siddhāntī).
For the Left is the scripture of Śambhu, while the Right is of the nature of Bhairava.
The *Miśra* is said to be the *Yāmala*, having seven measures as its primary feature;
indeed, the *Siddhānta* is remembered as the *Śuddhaśaiva*, the essence of all.
The Vāma, the Dakṣiṇa, and the Miśraka—these three are declared to be outside of Śaivism; they are not honored even within the Śaiva fold.
The Śaiva system is declared to be fourfold, while the Siddhānta is of two kinds:
namely, Karmānta and Jñānānta; the supreme Śaiva is remembered as being above these.
Conduct and ritual action indeed constitute the means for accomplishing karmas;
then, for the knower, conduct and ritual action become joined with yoga. (26)
The Śaiva [system] is to be known as higher than the highest, the sole leader of all tantras;
it is to be known as consisting of all tantras and as being composed of all mantras. || 27 ||
Through austerities performed in previous births, the arising of knowledge of the true path occurs;
he is the preceptor, the practitioner of mantra, the putraka, and the samayin.
These four may be Śaivas, whether they are ascetics or householders;
for all castes alike, there is the practice of the Śiva-mantra. (29)
In the Śivadharmottara, it was stated by Śiva for the sake of dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation:
"Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a woman, a Śūdra, or likewise one belonging to an āśrama," (30)
The householder, the mendicant, likewise the student, and the forest-dweller—these are declared to be the stages of life (āśramas). || 31 ||
There are four sacred precincts (gocaras) of Śambhu, which have emerged directly from his own form:
the Śiva-gotra, the Śikhā-gotra, and the Jyotis-gotra as the third. (32)
Sāvitrī-gotra—these four constitute the Śaiva-gotra;
those who act for the benefit of the world are to be known as Śaivas, and no others.
Arising from pure causes and endowed with knowledge and action,
Dadhīci established that place which is remembered as Govidāra.
The sacred site named Āmardaka, frequented by the illustrious Dūrvāsas, is located there; from that place emerged the sites Raṇabhadra and Golaka. (35)
Those Śaivas who have arisen from this place are of four kinds:
the student (brahmacārī), the householder (gṛhastha), the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), and likewise the ascetic (yati). || 36 ||
For these as well, renunciation is prescribed for those who are fit and principal;
having been initiated, one should enter the renunciate stage of life (saṃnyāsa-āśrama), which is exceedingly supreme. (37)

Therefore, O twice-born ones, there is no liberation from vows for one who effects absolute isolation (*kaivalya*); rather, in this world, those whose faces are turned toward liberation [attain it] through contact with the knowledge known as initiation (*dīkṣā*). (38)

Giving is of four kinds: obligatory, occasional, for a specific desire, and pure; it should be bestowed upon a worthy recipient (pātra), but not even the slightest amount should be given to one who is not a worthy recipient.
That gift which is always given without aiming for a fruit is called "eternal" (nitya) by Śambhu, the God of gods. (40)
That gift which is bestowed with faith for the purpose of purifying evil is declared by the seers who proclaim the Vedas to be *naimittika* (occasional) charity. (41)

Whatever gift is given with devotion for the sake of a son, for the sake of spiritual attainment, or for the sake of heaven—since it is performed without [regard for the ultimate goal]—it is designated as "kāmya" (motivated by desire). || 42 ||
That gift which is given out of devotion to Śiva for the sake of pleasing Hara is declared to be the supreme gift; it is the sole means for attaining liberation. (43)
(57) One should indicate everything declared by the architect, the cord-holder, the carpenter, and likewise the wood-wright, according to the Śiva-śāstra. || 44 ||
The son named Viśvakarman is called the *sthapati* (master builder);
his son, the offspring of Maya, is celebrated as the *sūtragrāhin* (line-holder). || 45 ||
The son of the divine sage Aṣṭa is celebrated as Vardhakī; the son of Mānu is named Takṣaka, who has four offspring beginning with Sthapati. (46)
One who constructs palaces and the like is also known here as a *sthapati*;
a *vardhakī* is one who holds the measuring line, knows the measurements, and seeks out materials.
That which is fit for thinning and refining is called *dakṣaka*;
it cuts through all things that are to be cut, and it breaks apart substances that are to be split. (48)

The materials for the ritual should be understood through the middle [section], while the work of the artisans is threefold: the master builder (sthapati), the string-measurer (sūtragrāhī), and those who fashion the temple, images, and so forth. (49)
One should perform the rites beginning with the opening of the eyes using the right hand;
however, in all mantra-rituals, one should always avoid doing so with the remaining [left] hand.
But for the remaining work of the artisans, they must be appointed by the sthāpaka; in those artisanal tasks, they act according to the direction of the sthāpaka. || 51 ||
The master builder should be knowledgeable in the scriptures and practical work, accomplished in his craft, and of noble birth;
he must not have missing limbs nor excessively red limbs, and he should be most righteous and truthful in speech. (52)
One who is endowed with knowledge of the fruit, virtuous, firm in his bonds, and not fickle—
such an artisan should be employed when beginning the construction of a temple that is pleasing in every way. (53)

The linga is to be known as fourfold, as prescribed in the scriptures: the stationary (sthāvaram), the divine (daivikam), the ṛṣi-made (ārṣakam), and likewise the human (mānuṣam) and the gaṇa-made (gāṇavam). || 54 ||
Thus, the fourfold characteristic of the divine [liṅga] has been stated; now hear the description of its features:
the liṅga should be elongated in shape and endowed with both depressions and elevations. (55)
Joined with lines and hollows, with a stream at the opening as high as a mountain peak, it was fashioned with a cavity and many knotted crests.
With both hands joined in the shape of a hollowed casket and devoid of the sacred thread (brahmasūtra)—endowed with these characteristics, it is called the divine (daivika) linga. || 57 ||
The base of the liṅga should be thick, and likewise its top;
however, the middle of the liṅga should be thick, having the shape of a coconut fruit.

That liṅga, which resembles the fruit of the plantain tree and has the shape of the fruit of the bilva tree, is declared to be of the Ṛṣis (Ārṣa), and it is devoid of the sacred thread (brahmasūtra). || 59 ||
Resembling the fruit of the *kuśmāṇḍa*, having the shape of a *mātuluṅga* fruit, having the form of a cucumber, and resembling the fruit of the *kapittha*. || 60 ||
Likewise, the Gaṇeśa-liṅga is said to have the shape of a palmyra fruit;
it may be the size of the door, or the size of the sanctum, or even the size of a cubit. || 61 ||
Or [the head] may have the proportions prescribed in the treatises on craftsmanship (*śilpiśāstra*), with its top rising in the shape of an umbrella;
this head should be of this color, glossy, and provided with the *brahmasūtra*. (62)
Thus, a human *liṅga* is said to be endowed with these characteristics:
the first is the *sarvatobhadra*, and the second is the *vartamānaka*.
The third is the superiority of Śaivism, and the fourth is the three-fold classification;
thus, the fourfold Liṅga is declared to be the Mahāliṅga.
Each one has four divisions, and each one is of four kinds;
thus, the *liṅga* is proclaimed in summary to be of sixty-four types. (65)
The thousand-fold stream Liṅga, such as the four-formed (Caturmūrti) Liṅga and others, is proclaimed as the Mahāliṅga; it is the thousand-fold Dhārāliṅga.
The Nāgara, Sarvatobhadra, Drāviḍa, Vartamānaka, Śivādhikya, Vesara, and Trairāśika are the mixed types. (67)
One should gradually install the fourfold linga according to the prescribed rites;
a wise man should install thousands of dhārā-lingas in the Miśraka shrine.

The seat, the bed, the standing place, and the vehicle—these are the fourfold [types]. They know that the vehicle belongs to the goddesses and the like, while the standing place belongs to human beings. (69)
The seat of Svāyambhuva is for those who are seated; for others, there may be a reclining posture. The Linga and the seat situated in the present state are superior to Śiva. (70)
The vehicle should be known as consisting of three parts, and the bed as having equal sections;
therein, the head-cushion should be of this fourfold kind. (71)
It is shaped like a hen’s egg, and likewise like an umbrella;
it has a form resembling a crescent moon, and indeed the shape of a bubble. (72)
For Brahmins it is shaped like a bubble; for kings, it is variegated;
for Vaiśyas, it resembles a crescent moon; and for Śūdras, it is like a hen’s egg.
The head of all men possesses a mark shaped like an umbrella; O King, it is ordained that for every Brahmin, there are three such umbrella-shaped marks.
O Hari, two [marks] resembling the half-moon are thus proclaimed for the Vaiśyas;
for Śūdras, O Hari, only one is said, which resembles a hen's egg.
The [sequence] ending with the lamp, ending with the sacrificial oblation (havir), ending with the offering (bali), and ending with the tāṇḍava dance;
the ten-fold service (daśopacāra) ending with the lamp, and the sixteen-fold service ending with the sacrificial oblation. 76.
The offering of bali concludes at the twenty-fifth [verse], and the tāṇḍava dance at the thirty-sixth.
Likewise, there is the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth, as well as the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya).
Bathing, perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and the ritual dismissal—
this is the worship of Śiva consisting of ten services (daśopacāra), beginning with bathing and ending with the lamp.
Having likewise performed the invocation, he should offer water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya;
then the bath, clothing, the sacred thread, ornaments, fragrance, and flowers. (79)
Incense, lamps, and food offerings, as well as prostration and dismissal—these constitute the sixteen modes of service; such is the worship ending with the sacrificial oblation. (80)
Having performed the invocation, as well as the ritual placement and the formal welcome,
[he should offer] water for the feet, water for sipping, the respectful offering (arghya), a new garment, and an upper cloth.
Ornaments, perfumes, and flowers, as well as incense and lamps, collyrium for the eyes, sacred ash, a fly-whisk, and a palm-leaf fan. || 82 ||
The vision of the ten mudrās, the worship of the five coverings, the food offering, the rite of fire oblation, and the fivefold presentation of the bali offering. (83)
The measure of recitation and praise, dance, song, and rhythm, as well as water and the marriage ceremony— these constitute the thirty-six modes of service (upacāra).
The limbs, the minor limbs, the major limbs, and the subsidiary limbs—these four constitute the body.
The head, the face, and the heart are proclaimed to be the limbs (aṅga). || 85 ||

The chest, the throat, the breasts, the arms, as well as the navel, the private parts, the abdomen, and the pair of thighs and knees—these are proclaimed to be the individual limbs (pratyaṅga). || 86 ||
The eyes, the tip of the nose, the ears, the hands, the soles of the feet, the toes, the matted hair, and the crown—these are proclaimed as the limbs. || 87 ||
Seats, ornaments, and so forth are proclaimed as the secondary limbs (upāṅga);
these must be fashioned for all the complete forms (sakala) within the child-image (bālabimba). 88.
p.
62) Or else, a young man [should fashion] an image or a pedestal made of brick;
that which reaches to the knees is declared the smallest, while that which reaches to the arms would be the middle-sized. || 89 ||
This is declared to be the supreme measurement for the characteristics of a small image;
the wise man should install either the image or its pedestal before the deity.
In this case, there may be a breach of the mantra, but no breach of the ritual action;
for all [the mantras], even when their individual limbs and so forth are cut or broken, they remain effective.
Having performed the measurement according to the previously stated characteristics, one should then perform the yoga-measurement;
there, one should fashion the secret [mandala] and again carry out the re-consecration.
In the case of the deities beginning with Umā and Skanda, when they are depicted as being devoid of their powers and weapons,
the wise one should, as before, have an auspicious image fashioned together with their respective powers.
If, when the time has passed due to negligence, one performs all the festivals and other rites with worship, offerings of food, and so forth, it becomes the abode of Rākṣasas. (94)
Just as one who possesses a body casts off what is worn out and takes up another, therefore, with every effort, one should have [the temple] renovated after removing what is decayed. 95.
The fourfold [reckoning] consists of the Sāvana, the lunar (Cāndra), the stellar (Nakṣatra), and the solar (Saura).
The lunar month is proclaimed as ending with the new moon (darśānta) and ending with the full moon (paurṇamānta). || 96 ||
The solar measure is defined as the end of a zodiacal sign, while the civil (sāvana) measure is considered to be thirty days;
the lunar mansion month is said to begin with Aśvinī and end with the full moon.
The calculation of the lifespan, the ripening of karma, rites such as expiatory ceremonies,
and likewise the wages of servants, must all be performed using the *sāvana* [day] alone. (98)
In the solar month, the purifying festival of Sālya should be observed;
likewise, Śakti and Maṅgala are to be performed in the Sāvana, Cāndra, and Nakṣatra months respectively.
These four kinds of festivals for Śiva, dedicated to the sacred bathing sites (tīrthas) of the month, grant liberation;
moreover, in the lunar month, the [specific] constellation destroys all sins.

The solar month is known to increase progeny, while the sāvana month is remembered as conducive to peace; the lunar month, which concludes with the sacred tithis as its primary element, is declared to be the most excellent. (101)
O Guha, when the lunar mansion of a month is conjoined with the full moon every month, that festival in the Sāvana calendar should be known as the Pratiṣṭhotsava.

Likewise, month by month, one should know that the lunar mansion of the month is deficient and equal [to the day's mansion], and avoid it accordingly, O best of the twice-born, if it is the lunar mansion of a sacred ford (tīrtha).
When two lunar mansions (nakṣatras) coincide within a single month, the latter is most excellent;
however, the first mansion is not desired, for one should perform the pilgrimage at the other mansion.
If it is performed under one's own birth-constellation (nakṣatra), the performer of that rite perishes;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform the pilgrimage at a different constellation.
Musical instruments are proclaimed to be of four kinds:
the struck (tata), the stretched (vitata), the solid (ghana), and the hollow (suṣira). || 106 ||

The *tata* (stretched) is said to be the lute (*vīṇā*) and so forth; the *vitata* (expanded) is the mouth and so forth; the *ghana* (solid) is the bronze cymbals (*kāṃsyatāla*) and so forth; and likewise, the *suṣira* (hollow) is the flute (*vaṃśa*) and so forth. (107)
The mind is said to be fourfold; hear now its divisions:
the conjoined (saṃsṛṣṭa), the inert (baliman), the distracted (vikṣipta), and that which goes and returns (gatāgati).
Even while grasping objects, cognition attains the state of being an object of knowledge;
yet it is not actually joined with them—that is what is described as "conjunction" (saṃsṛṣṭi). || 109 ||
Neither the mind, nor that which is to be thought, nor the thinker is perceived;
completely withdrawn and liberated from sense objects, one becomes unified like one in deep sleep.
Since one who is devoted to sense objects is surpassed by the man of knowledge,
he who is constantly agitated throughout the three periods of time is said to be distracted.
From ignorance one goes to knowledge, and from knowledge one indeed goes to ignorance;
he who wavers through weakness undergoes this coming and going.
Among those, the one who is completely withdrawn is the highest, transcending the qualities (guṇas) and free from affliction;
he who is moderately so should be known as the middle, while he who is intensely thrilled is considered to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
The middling and the lowest are the coming and going of the rājasa state;
the fourth, however, is the distracted state of the tāmasa type, for it is the most base.
The meditator, the meditation, the object of meditation, or else the purpose of meditation—having understood this tetrad, one should practice yoga like a yogi. (115)

One who possesses the perfection of knowledge and dispassion, endowed with faith and forbearance, a devotee of Śiva, and always full of enthusiasm— this is remembered as the Puruṣa to be meditated upon. (116)
In the meditation on the inconceivable, one should repeatedly meditate with mindfulness upon Śiva;
through perfectly purified knowledge, this is known as the meditation on knowledge (jñāna-dhyāna). || 117 ||
The Lord, who is complete, whose body is tranquil, omniscient, and all-pervading,
is to be meditated upon through various conceptual forms for the sake of attaining spiritual perfection.
Liberation preceded by the causal conditions, as well as sovereignty consisting of the powers such as *aṇimā*—these two should be known as the purposes for the meditation on Śiva. (119)
It is also said here that, according to the sequence beginning with the True Path (sanmārga), it is fourfold:
the True Path, the Path with [the Teacher], the Path of the Ancestors, and the other.
In the fourth stage, the disciple is indeed called the servant-path;
they know the paths of conduct, service, and the son in their respective order. (121)
Śiva has established the Sahamārga, the Yogapāda, the Sanmārga, and Jñāna itself; likewise, he established the Dāsamārga, meditation (dhyāna), and the temples of the Liṅga and Bimba.
He was a dancer and actress in the Śaiva tradition, a singer of hymns, and a crusher of enemies;
he followed the path of his son, was devoted to the worship of Śiva and other rites, and was intent upon recitation and fire-offerings.
The *praveśaka* is indeed the instruction regarding the state of one who possesses the knowledge of Śiva;
it is that very path of union for those who are experts in the Śaiva Āgamas.

He who has adopted all beings as his own children, who is noble, who belongs to the lineage of the Buddhas, who follows the true path, and who possesses equanimity and purity— he is called a worldly being (saṃsārī). (125)
One who is equanimous, free from egoism, and has exerted effort in the knowledge of Śiva—this fourfold path bestows fruits such as *sālokya* and the rest. (126)
Sālokya, Sāmīpya, Sārūpya, and likewise Sāyujya—having attained the world through meditation, Sālokya is prescribed for that [level]. || 127 ||
That which is situated near a particular place is called "proximity" (sāmīpya);
the attainment of that specific form is known as "conformity" (sārūpya). || 128 ||
When Śiva is united, that form is called *sāyujya* (union);
when all bonds have dissolved and the *āṇava* power has been liberated. (129)
The power that illuminates everything unfolds everywhere, just like that of Śiva. || 129½ ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Śiva exists in five states: as the manifest (sakala), the unmanifest (niṣkala), the manifest-unmanifest (sakalaniṣkala), and as the subtle and the differentiated (sūkṣmabhinna). || 1 ||
(67) He who is endowed with the *kalās* such as Śānti and the rest is recited as *sakala* (with parts);
he who is alone, even beyond the *bindu*, is *niṣkala* (without parts), yet [he is also] *sakalaniṣkala*.
Joined with Jvālinī and the others, this subtle point (bindu) is so called;
differentiated by the sixteen vowels, the bindu is said to be manifold in nature.
He pervades the entire world and pervades it along with all embodied beings;
because he is situated everywhere, he is known as Sakala (the Whole). || 4 ||
He is beyond the distinctions of time and non-time, has attained equanimity everywhere;
He is free from conceptual proliferation, devoid of appearance, stainless, partless, and auspicious.
That reality situated in the void is devoid of both the signified and the signifier;
transcending the causal kalās, it is indeed called the partless (niṣkala).
That which is the supreme form, the body of mantra, is exceedingly so;
one should know that supreme form to be both with parts and without parts.
That subtle atom is situated in the center of the heart;
it causes the entire universe to vibrate, and it is indeed proclaimed as the Subtle One (Sūkṣma). || 8 ||

That form which consists of the essence of the mantra, beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa', is divided in many ways; he who is thus differentiated is called "sakala" (with parts).
Know that within this knowledge imparted by others there are five categories:
the bound soul (paśu), Vāgīśvara, Vidyā, Yoni, and liberation (mukti) as the final stage. 10.
And likewise, in the Raurava [Tantra], five categories are proclaimed:
first is that called Śivasāda, and the second is Amūrti. (11)
The third is called Mūrtisāda, the fourth is named Kartṛ, and the fifth is Karmasāda; thus is the pentad of Sādākhya.
The characteristics of Karma and Sādākhyā are according to the manner of the Liṅga and the Pīṭha;
Nāda and Bindu are to be known, and this is declared as the Bindupīṭha. (13)
The form endowed with *nāda* and *bindu* is called *karma-sādākhya*;
the four [levels] beginning with the form of the agent (*kartṛ-rūpa*) are said to be *nāda* alone.
That which is the nature of the agent known as Sādākhya, resting upon Mūrti and the others, indeed rests upon Mūrti and the others by means of the remainder known as Pañcasādākhya. || 15 ||
The form of the ritual action (karmarūpa), resting sequentially upon the agent and the other factors, should have Karmeśa as its eastern face and the agent’s [face] on the right side. || 16 ||
The form with a western face is Mūrti, and the one with a northern face is Amūrti;
Śiva’s Sādākhya is above—thus they know him as five-faced.
Because it is eternally of the nature of Śiva, it is celebrated as Sādākhya;
Svayambhū is the formless Bāṇaliṅga known as Sādākhya-Śiva. || 18 ||
The human is called Karmasāda, the divine is named Kartṛsāda, and Maheśa is named Mūrtisāda; these five are said to be Sādākhya.
(69) First is Mūrti-brahman; second is Tattva-brahman;
third is Bhūta-brahman; and fourth is Piṇḍa-brahman. || 20 ||
The fifth is proclaimed as Kalābrahman and Pañcabrahman;
because it consists of all [five] together, it is called Mūrtibrahman.
Among all the principles (tattvas), the principle of Śiva is remembered as the sovereign;
therefore, the Self, beginning with the Pure (śuddha) and so forth, is proclaimed as the Brahman of the principles. 22.
The first would be the seed of flesh; the second arises from fat;
the third is the sixth variety, and likewise the fourth is the seventh.
One should know that each of these five is composed of the five elements;
indeed, flesh is the seed of the earth element, while fat is said to be that of water.
The sixth is declared to be fire (tejas), the seventh consists of wind (māruta),
the fifth is the seed-syllable of space (vyoma), and this is proclaimed as the Brahma of the elements (bhūtabrahman).
Beginning with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), followed by one's own name in the dative case, and joined at the end with "namas," it is called "sadyādi" in its proper sequence. (26)
The syllables of the individual soul (jīva) within the syllables of Śiva, through their conjunction, are called the Piṇḍa.
Because it is the form of the Piṇḍa, the Lord of Karma is also declared to be the Piṇḍabrahman.
The kalās of Īśāna are five; those of Puruṣa are four;
the kalās of Aghora are eight; and there are thirteen in Vāmadeva. (28)
The eight immediate *kalās* are to be known; they are proclaimed as the *kalā-brahman*.
Likewise, the principle of form (*mūrti-tattva*), the elemental state (*bhūta*), the body (*piṇḍa*), and the *kalā* itself [are to be understood]. (29)
One should employ these five Brahmans in all ritual activities;
they are traditionally known as Mantra-Brahman, Kriyā-Brahman, and Tattva-Brahman. || 30 ||
The seed-syllable, Brahmā, Mukha-Brahmā, and Pañca-Brahmā are thus proclaimed; namely, Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, and Vāma. (31)
That which is proclaimed as Sadyojāta is also remembered as Mantrabrahman;
[it is employed for] invocation (āvāhana), installation (sthāpana), presence (sānnidhya), and confinement (sannirodhana). || 32 ||
This is called the *avakuṇṭhana*; it is remembered as the Brahman of Action (*kriyā-brahma*).
[It consists of] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. || 33 ||
These five types are declared; that reality is remembered as Brahman. [It consists of] the letter *la*, the letter *va*, the letter *ra*, and the letter *ya*. (34)
The letter *ha* is said to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and it is remembered as the Seed-Brahman (*bījabrahma*). It consists of Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Puruṣa, and Īśāna. (35)
These five types are declared; they are remembered as "Mukhabrahman.
Thus, because of these five divisions, it is illustrated as "Pañcabrahma" (the Five Brahmas). || 36 ||
Śāntyātītā, Śānti, Vidyā, Sthiti, and Nivṛtti—these are the five worlds known as Mahat-tejas which Śiva obtains. (37)
Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jātārthika in sequence—
these are the states of Sadāśiva, which rest upon the locus of enjoyment (bhogasthāna). (38)
The auspicious Nityā, consisting of five forms, is both with parts and without parts;
she is to be known as the form of Sadāśiva, the initiator of all activities. (39)
Thus, these five are the mantras; by them Śiva has his body bound.
In reality, however, they are not distinct, because he is non-different from his own power.
The Śivāstra, the Kṣurikāstra, as well as the Pāśupatāstra, the Vyomāstra, and the Aghorāstra—these are proclaimed as the five weapons. || 41 ||
The six-syllabled mantra is the weapon of Śiva; the eight syllables are the Razor (Kṣurikā);
the nine-syllabled is known as the Pāśupata; and the sky-weapon (Vyomāstra) consists of ten syllables. (42)

The Aghorāstra consists of forty [syllables]; thus, the five-fold weapon (pañcāstra) is described as bestowing liberation, increasing prosperity, fulfilling desires, and performing rites for peace and nourishment.
One should know the five-syllabled mantra as liberation, the six-syllabled as prosperity;
one should know the eight-syllabled as that for desired objects, and the nine-syllabled as pacification.
The nourishing [mantra] consists of ten seed-syllables; thus the mantra is remembered as being of five types.
These five kinds of mantras have been declared, beginning with the five-syllabled one. (45)
Thus the mantra has been fully explained; now hear the ritual placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa).
At the time of installing the liṅga, one should place the mantras of the principles (tattvas).
The mantras contained within the jars, the *liṅga*, and those full offerings— indeed,
that state resulting from the performance of their union is proclaimed as *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration). || 47 ||
Having understood the conjunction of the vital breath (prāṇa) and primordial nature (prakṛti), one should begin the installation;
this is declared to be the "vital breath mantra" (prāṇamantra), while primordial nature is said to be the "form" (mūrti). (48)
Because of the perfect union with the mantra-form, it is the cause for the presence of the deity;
therefore, one should indeed install the mantra-form within the center of the liṅga. (49)
One should place the pure root mantra on the crown; the thread-mantra should be in the middle; having placed the reality-mantra on the right, one should place the *dā*-mantra on the left.
The wise one should place himself at the base of the thread; this is called the placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa). Now, the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa) is described here.
One should place Karmeśa in front; one should install Kartṛ on the left side.
One should place Mūrti on the west and install Amūrti on the north.
Above that, one should place the five principles known as Śiva and Sādākhya;
[one should meditate upon] the God who consists of the five forms and is the cause of all causes. 53.
Endowed with the thirty-eight kalās and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa in the center,
one should then invoke the God by means of the five-syllabled mantra.
The wise one should perform the installation with the six-syllabled mantra;
perform the invocation of presence with the eight-syllabled mantra. (55)
One should perform the confinement with the nine-syllable mantra and fill [the vessel] with the ten seed-syllables;
the wise one should offer water for the feet, fragrance, and other offerings together with the Brahma-aṅgas.
At the time of establishing the whole [deity], one should place that seed-syllable in the heart;
it is said to be the "body of action" (kriyā-śarīra), and the mantra is traditionally known as the "life-force" (jīva). || 57 ||
Through the application of the sequence of ritual actions, Śiva-attainment is the cause;
therefore, having understood the living body, one should perform the rites. 58.
First there should be the purification of oneself; second, the purification of the site;
third, the purification of the ritual materials; and fourth, the purification of the mantra. || 59 ||
The fifth is the purification of the *liṅga*; thus, five purifications are taught.
First is the seat called Ananta, and after that, the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*).
The third is the yogic posture (yogāsana); after that, the lotus posture (padmāsana) follows;
the fifth is declared to be the pure one (vimala); one should arrange them in order above.
That which is endowed with eight seats is called the Anantāsana;
it consists of the fourfold [powers]: dharma, jñāna, vairāgya, and aiśvarya. || 62 ||
All [the postures] have the luster of royal conduct; that which is described as the lion-throne (siṃhāsana) is known as the yoga-posture (yogāsana), having a form like pure action.
The ninefold group of powers beginning with Vāmā is known as the lotus posture (padmāsana).
One should worship Gaṇāmbikā in the north and Mahādevī in the east.
p.
74) "Tanno Gaurī" in the south and "Vāruṇī" in the west—one should impel [the mantra] with these words.
Together with these Śaktis, one should conceive of the pure seat (vimalāsana). || 65 ||
The square and the circular are said to be the varieties of the pedestal (piṇḍikā);
each one is declared to be fivefold according to the distinctions of the square and so forth.
Bhadrā, Yakṣī, Vajrī, Śrīkarā, and Vijayā; Padmā, Cakrā, Vedī, Saumyā, and Ramyā as the fifth. || 67 ||
O beautiful one, I shall describe according to their true nature the Self, the Inner Self, the Outer Self, the Selfless, and the Supreme Self.
Relying upon that which is equal to Pradhāna, free from pleasure and pain, and established therein—O Goddess, he whose self is that very thing is called "of that nature" (tadātman). || 69 ||
Through its association with the city of eight, it wanders through all wombs;
that inner self is to be known as being bound by auspicious and inauspicious deeds. (70)
O Goddess, joined with the organs of intellect and action and enveloped by the great elements,
the external self is then always an enjoyer of experiences through its steadfastness.
Freed from the states of being and non-being, yet possessed of the impurity of karma regarding reality;
the self is rendered such that it is joined solely with the impurity of karma, its intellect fixed upon the nature of Māyā. || 72 ||
Then the Goddess is called Nirātmā (the Selfless One) by the Lord;
for she is indeed the Ātman, the Antarātman, and the Paramātman. 73.

And having realized that very reality, one is proclaimed as the *bhūtātman*; the *ātmabhūta* follows next, and immediately after that, the *antarātman*, which resides within the staff of the self. (74)
The Supreme Self (Paramātman) is situated in the center of the lotus; the Essential Self (Tattvātman) is on the right side;
the Elemental Self (Bhūtātman) is on the left side; and the Fivefold Self (Pañcātman) occupies the very place [of the center]. || 75 ||
The wise one, knowing the self as the elements, should again burn the womb-born;
the self as reality, being the prior immortality, and the pure self should likewise bring it to an end.
The Sakala possesses a subtle body, while the Pralayākala indeed does not;
the Vijñānakevala is pure—thus the person (puruṣa) is said to have five states. || 77 ||
The person (puruṣa) is proclaimed to be conjoined with the five sheaths;
therefore, he is neither the Vijñānākala nor the Pralayakevala.
Since one who is freed from ignorance and the rest attains the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha), therefore this entire [reality] receives the name "Purusha. (79)
Because he nourishes primordial nature (prakṛti), he is therefore called Puruṣa;
the entire world consists of impurity, action, the Great Illusion (mahāmāyā), and Māyā as its purpose.
Then, by the command of that [Power], the fivefold group—the power that causes concealment—acts like a meteor, remaining at their respective ends again and again as a bond. 81.
The Self creates the three worlds in an instant;
it is the movement within movement, as well as withdrawal (nivṛtti), establishment (pratiṣṭhā), knowledge (vidyā), and peace (śānti) immediately thereafter.
(76) Beyond Peace (śāntyatītā)—these five arise in the region of Nāda:
Kalā, Vidyā, Rāga, Kāla, and Niyati. 83.
And these five principles, O best of the twice-born, are of the nature of illusion (māyā);
they are the sheaths of the self consisting of food, vital breath, mind, and knowledge. (84)
And the sheaths consisting of bliss are declared to be the five sheaths;
O Goddess, they consist of food and the rest, each being subtler than the other.
For those who maintain that form is endowed with a self, the cause of its material substrate is illusion;
yet here, within the five sheaths, proponents wander in error, perceiving it as a self.
The wise know that bliss consists of those [states] produced by mental modifications;
indeed, the materialist (Lokāyata) holds that the self consists of the body made of food. (87)
Those who are struck by the stream of delusion know the vital breath (prāṇa), which is transformed by the physical bodies, to be composed of Māyā;
they grasp the self as consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya) and nothing else. || 88 ||
Some Vedic scholars have declared the Self to consist of bliss;
most, however, say it transcends the nature of the ego and consists of mind.

The word *skandha* signifies a collection (*samūha*) of cognitions (*jñāna*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), perceptions (*saṃjñā*), feelings (*vedanā*), and forms (*rūpa*); or it denotes the continuum (*santati*) of each of those. (90)
In this context, the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is said to be the very continuum of cognition;
and the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) is said to be the endless continuum of latent impressions (vāsanā). 91.
The intellect (buddhi) consists of pleasure and pain; from that [intellect] arises the self which is dependent upon them.
This is called the "aggregate" (skandha) of the Vedas, which is the very meaning of the term "aggregate."
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is that wherein exists the continuity of material entities;
it consists of five parts: the raw, the cooked, the impurity, the womb, and the bladder.
His state consists of five stages; his own vision and action are obstructed by impurity (mala). His senses are expanded, yet he is not himself [independent], for even he is [governed] by Śambhu.
One should know that the waking state is at the mouth, while the dream state is near the heart;
beginning from the heart and extending to the navel is the state of deep sleep.
Below that is the fourth state (turya), and the one beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is the subtle body (liṅgaka).
Thus, the waking state and so forth are said here to be the instigators of the dream state.
In the waking state there are thirty-five [kalās], in this dream state twenty-five;
in deep sleep there are those known as the forms (mūrtis), and in the fourth state (turya) there is a pair, respectively. 97.
In the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), there is the One; one should contemplate the Self therein.
However, I shall speak this secret—listen, O Nandikeśvara! (98)
The gross, the subtle, the very subtle, and that which is subtler than even that;
the gross is to be known as the waking state, while the subtle here is called the dreaming state. (99)

Deep sleep (suṣupti) is extremely subtle, while the fourth state (turyaka) is exceedingly subtle; beyond that is the transcendent (atīta). Thus, [the Self] is traditionally remembered as being fivefold.
(78) That which has passed through the five states, beginning with waking, is of the nature of consciousness;
its certainty is attained solely through the light of the True Guru’s instruction. || 101 ||
Celibacy, recitation, silence, patience, and moderation in food—this is the reading variation (*kṣāntirnāharalāsavam*).
Such is the form of austerity, most formidable, characterized by these five features. (102)
The Ādiśaivas, Mahāśaivas, Anuśaivas, Antaraśaivas, and Avāntaraśaivas—these five are briefly declared by the Śaivas. (103)
Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, and likewise Īśvara—these are known as the Anādi-śaivas; now hear of the Mahāśaivas.
The eight great lords of knowledge (vidyeśvaras), beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin;
the lords of mantras (mantreśvaras) and the mantras themselves; and those born in the same region as the great Śaivas. || 105 ||
Established within the principles (tattvas) from Māyā down to the earth, those disciples of Ananta who possess the nature of Rudra are proclaimed as the Ādiśaivas. || 106 ||
The gods, such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu; likewise the Daityas, humans, sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Uragas, and so forth—(all these were born). || 107 ||
All those disciples of Śrīkaṇṭha, as well as Umādevī and the other Śaktis, are declared to be these Anuśaivas; now hear of those intermediate ones and their observances.
(79) The four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, [attained their status] by the grace of the Supreme Lord;
likewise the sages Dūrvāsas and Agastya, and those born of the lineage of the sage Dadhīci. || 109 ||
These intermediate [categories] have been declared as Śaivas who follow the state of Śiva;
now, the Śaiva [system] has been fully explained according to the Śivāgama.
The first is the Anādi-Śaiva; he alone is Śiva himself when [he manifests as such].
Those who were initiated by Sadāśiva at the very beginning are the Ādi-Śaivas.
Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Bhāradvāja, Gautama, and Agastya—these five were initiated into the five faces. || 112 ||
The third is the Mahāśaiva; he is called a Śaiva Brahmin. The fourth is the Anuśaiva, who is traditionally known as a king or a Vaiśya. || 113 ||
This fifth intermediate state is indeed called the Śūdra;
it consists of the worldly, the Vedic, and likewise the spiritual. (114)
Excessive pride and what is called mantra; furthermore, the division of tantra is fivefold: the worldly, astrology, the Vedic, and likewise logic (nyāya). 115.
The Adhyātmavaidika is proclaimed [as one], while the Atimārga is the Raudraka;
the Śuddhaśaiva is known as Mantra—these are the five that have emerged from the Five Faces.
The bull among sages [composed] the collection of logical principles for determining the scriptures:
the Sūtra, the Bhāṣya, the Vārtika, as well as the Vyākhyā and the Prakaraṇa. || 117 ||
(80) Grant me the state of having five knots; those who know them understand the knots thus:
[a definition] with few syllables, free from doubt, substantial, and facing in all directions. (118)
Those who know the sūtras understand a sūtra to be that which is free from redundancy and irreproachable;
therein the great tree of the meaning of the mantra is established like a seed. (119)
The *ālāpamūlasūtra* is adorned with the word "atha" and others;
it is that wherein the meaning of the sūtra is explained through sentences that follow the sūtra. (120)
The *svīpadāni* are described; those who know the *bhāṣya* recognize it as such.

(There is a variant reading: *sthāpadā*). [The components are: the division of words (*padaccheda*), the statement of word-meanings (*padārthokti*), the analysis (*vigraha*), and the syntactic construction (*vākyayojanā*). || 121 ||

An objection, a resolution, and an explanation constitute the fivefold characteristics [of a commentary], wherein reflection upon what has been stated, what has not been stated, what has been repeated twice, and so forth, proceeds. (122)
Wise scholars who know the *vārtika* call that work a *vārtika*, which is established upon a specific portion of a treatise and situated within another task of that treatise. (123)

Those who are experts in the divisions of the scriptures say that a *prakaraṇa* (section) consists of the primary creation (*sarga*), the secondary creation (*pratisarga*), the genealogies (*vaṃśa*), and the periods of the Manvantaras (*manvantarāṇi*). || 124 ||
Having recited the genealogical history and the Purāṇa characterized by five marks,
the wise man should perform the division of words (padaccheda).

(81) Thus, the statement of the word-meanings follows; thereafter, the meaning of the syntactic connection (anvaya) is intended. This should be understood as "the compound" (samāsa); thus, listening (śravaṇa) is traditionally held to be fivefold. || 126 ||
The means of accomplishing the assistance, the analysis of place and time, and the remedy once [the situation] has been analyzed—this is also established as having five components. (127)

The "other" (para), the "great" (mahat), the "divine" (divya), the "both divine and non-divine" (divyādivya), and the "non-divine" (adivya)—these five types of relationships have been proclaimed. || 128 ||
And that [syllogism] here consists of five members: the proposition, the reason, the example, the application, and finally the conclusion as the fifth. (129)
The statement of the desired object is the proposition; my word possessing its pervasion is the reason;
the example is stated as being of that same kind; and the reason likewise awaits its counterpart. (130)
Furthermore, there may be the expansion and application of both the example and the subject;
then there is the restriction of the proposition, which constitutes the conclusion accompanied by its reason. || 131 ||
In another Śiva-āgama, five ornaments of logical reasons are taught;
the first reason is unestablished (asiddha), and the second is contradictory (viruddha). (132)
The third [category] is non-absolutism (anekānta), and likewise the fourth is the section on [the self].
The fifth is proclaimed as that which is designated by time and truth. || 133 ||
Pratiṣṭhā, sthāpana, sthiti, and sthāpana itself;
āsthāpana is declared as the fourth, and likewise utthāpana. || 134 ||
(82) The consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is to be known as fivefold; its determination is now declared.
Having first installed the *liṅga* within the *brahmaśilā*, [the process proceeds]. || 135 ||

Alternatively, when that which has the unmanifest as its face and sign is performed preceded by the binding of the pedestal, that shall be the *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration); furthermore, it is called *sthāpana* (installation). || 136 ||
A linga made of precious minerals or of iron, or even of stone, is established upon a pedestal;
that is declared to be "sthāpana" (establishment). || 137 ||
An unseparated pedestal is prescribed for the *liṅga* made of crystal and other such materials;
where the consecration is performed mentally, that is called *sthitasthāpana*.
Whether it be a manifest linga measuring four cubits or more, or even another type of linga, that in which the consecration rite is performed is called "installation" (āsthāpana). || 139 ||
When a linga that is defiled by defects such as being "vyaṅgya" (deficient) is carefully removed and installed elsewhere by someone else, that is called "utthāpana" (re-installation). || 140 ||
The egg-born, the hair-cut-born, the hair-grown, the skin-born, and likewise the left-born—these five are proclaimed as the types of beds for the couch. (141)
In this context, the "egg-born" (aṇḍaja) should be understood as that which originates from the five types of birds;
that which is made of cotton is proclaimed to be the "shorn-born" (muṇḍaja).
The woolen garment (*roja*) is known to be made from the hair of animals such as sheep;

that which is made from the skins of tigers, lions, and the like is called leathern (*carmaja*); and the silk garment (*kauśeya*) is known to be produced from the cocoon of the silkworm (*vāma*). || 143 ||
Somāskanda should come first; after that, Sukhāsana, Kalyāṇasundara, and Candraśekhara. (144)
Gaṅgādhara—these five are proclaimed as the forms of the Creator;
likewise Vṛṣabhavāhana and Ardhanārīśvara. || 145 ||
And Kirāta, as well as Vīreśa and Bhikṣāṭana beyond that;
these indeed are the five forms, declared to be the forms of persistence (sthitimūrti).
Irakṣaṇa, Virakṣaṇa, Dvirakṣaṇa, and Vicakṣaṇa—
these were his names, endowed with auspicious marks, given by Hastema.
The *irakṣaṇa* should be nine cubits, and the *dvirakṣaṇa* ten cubits;
the *dvirakṣaṇa* is for the number of Rudras (eleven), while the *vicakṣaṇa* is for the number of the Sun (twelve).
The enclosure wall, characterized by the number five, should be fivefold;
one should construct this enclosure all around according to the dimensions of the palace.
The width of the palace is called its staff (daṇḍa);
that which is made with half of the staff is the inner mandala itself.
In the case of a single-staffed inner enclosure, it is measured by two staffs at the middle enclosure;
however, when the measurement is four staffs, it is traditionally known as having established boundaries.
The wall of the great boundary should be seventeen *daṇḍas* in measure;
thus is the enclosure described, and the procedure for the gate-tower (*gopura*) is prescribed.
In the mandala, the door-decorations and the door-halls are [placed] upon the necklaces; in the central necklace of the palace, the boundary is called the mansion (harmya). (153)
Thus, in the Mahāmaryā, the gopura is remembered as being fivefold: [representing] the birth, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and liberation of the world. (154)
These five functions of such a one [the Lord] are performed while he is thus deluded;
this alone is proclaimed as the supreme divine *tāṇḍava*. (155)

The sacrifice of action, the sacrifice of austerity, the sacrifice of recitation, as well as the sacrifice of meditation, and then the sacrifice of knowledge—thus is the fivefold sacrifice proclaimed. (156)

Then, through various distinctions such as worship, fire-rituals, and so forth, the sacrifice of action (karmayajña) is fully described; austerity (tapas) consists of the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such practices. || 157 ||
The private recitation of the Śiva-mantra is declared to be "japa" by its designation;
the sacrifice of meditation is explained as the repeated contemplation of Śiva. (158)
Teaching, studying, explaining, listening, and reflecting—by these five modes, the sacrifices of knowledge are proclaimed. (159)
Because it is the most excellent of all sacrifices due to its innumerable great qualities,
therefore this [sacrifice] is pure and bestows the fruit of liberation.
Just as a mirror becomes stainless when it is constantly polished, so too does the intellect of men become stainless through the practice of knowledge. (161)
Through sacrifices one attains the state of a deity; through austerities, the status of a Brāhmaṇa;
through meditation, various enjoyments; and through knowledge, one shall attain liberation. || 162 ||
The teacher, the practitioner, the spiritual son, and the initiate—these five, according to the Māheśvara [tradition], are each superior in qualities to the preceding one. || 163 ||
Having respectfully ascertained the disciple's status according to the sequence beginning with Brāhmaṇa and so forth,
one should worship him during the auspicious rites for the gods, such as the Pavitrārohaṇa and others.
And among all these, the guide is declared to be the foremost;
he by whom it is proclaimed, "I am the guide," is the excellent Guru.
In the Śiva-āgama it is stated that the command of the preceptor and my own command are equal;
therefore, at the outset, he should be worshipped by all according to his merit.
The one established in the samaya is superior; from him, the *putraka* is superior; from the excellent *sādhaka*, the *ācārya* is the most excellent. (167)
The Rudrākṣa rosary, the sacred thread, the turban, the upper garment, and the sacred ash—these are proclaimed as the five insignia (mudrās) of the foremost Śaivas. || 168 ||
In the Siddhānta, however, those initiated Brāhmaṇas and others who abide by their vows all become wearers of the five mudrās in certain Āgamas. (169)
The seat, the yoga-band, the bamboo staff, the water-pot, and the rosary—these five constitute the fivefold equipment of the yogis. (170)
The water-pot, the earring, the serpent, the crest-jewel,
and the hair-sacrificial thread— these are the five mudrās in the Great Vow (mahāvrata). (171)
A golden ring, a bracelet, an armlet, an earring, as well as a golden sacred thread—these constitute the five-fold ornamentation. || 172 ||
The dancer, the drummer, the singer, the flute-player, and likewise the lute-player—these are proclaimed as the five teachers. || 173 ||
They were devoted to the purpose of harmonizing the four castes, diligent in the sequence of the Nāṭya-veda,
skilled in meditative cultivation, singing, and dancing, and proficient in the knowledge of instrumental music.
And those devotees of mine who are known as the nine types of dancers, being free from all taint, among them the dancer who knows the science of dance is declared to be the most excellent. (175)
The five teachers, my daughters, and the divine handmaidens were intent upon playing the lute with independent melodies and chanting mantras. || 176 ||

The specific excellence of these [deities] in sequence has been declared according to their respective functions; therefore, for others not mentioned here, it should be understood by following their particular activities. (177)
Nandā, Bhadrā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and likewise Sumanā—these five mothers of cows are established in the world of Śiva. (178)
Milk, curd, ghee, cow urine, and likewise cow dung—
this is declared to be the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), which destroys even the greatest sins.
If curd and milk are unavailable, there shall be milk; if milk is unavailable, there shall be curd.
If cow dung is unavailable, there shall be cow urine; if that is unavailable, however, there shall be cow dung. (180)
One should exert effort regarding the five products of the cow; in their absence, one may use whatever ghee is available.
One should perform this at the conclusion of initiation, at the conclusion of consecration, and at the conclusion of the pavitraka rite.
One should prepare the *brahmakūrca* according to the ritual procedure for the five products of the cow;
whoever drinks it with devotion shall attain union with Śiva.
On the eighth and fourteenth days of the lunar fortnight, and especially on the new moon day (the dark festival),
one should diligently perform the worship of Śiva, which is particularly dear to him.
Milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar, along with kuśa-water,
are declared to be the "five nectars" (pañcāmṛta), which destroy the five great sins.
In the absence of sugar, one should drink the essence of sugarcane; in the absence of honey, one should drink ghee.
One should prepare the stomach, the vessel, and the mantras as before. || 185 ||
The plantain, the jackfruit, the coconut fruit, the mango, and the citron—these are known as the five fruits. || 186 ||
Extraction from the right side, burning, filling with pure sand, and touching with the footprint of a cow—these five are the purifications of the site. (187)
Fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offering—these constitute the five-fold service (pañcopacāra); alternatively, it is also accepted as ending with the lamp.
The entry into the womb, the rite for a male child, the parting of the hair, the birth-rite,
and the naming of the fire— these constitute the five purificatory rites (saṃskāras). || 189 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which is known as the fivefold causal condition:
the auspicious causal condition of the fetter (pāśa), and likewise the causal condition of the bound soul (paśu). || 190 ||
Thereafter, the writing on palm leaves, as well as the ritual for the jar and the serpent, are declared to be the five-fold proof (pañcapratyaya). || 191 ||
For the sake of purifying truth and falsehood, the wise man should cause an ordeal to be administered;
the preceptor should always administer it on a Sunday and when the sun is in the sign of Aries.
Whatever substance one should offer for the sake of dharma, having pointed toward the truth; || 192 ½ ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
The Lord, knowledge, as well as ignorance, the bound soul, and the bond are the causes;
it is said that these cease to exist—thus one should practice the six categories of reality.

For the sake of the enjoyment and liberation of bound souls (paśu), he is remembered as Paśupati, the Attainer; this is because of the teaching on the three principles (stritattva) known as dissolution (laya), experience (bhoga), and authority (adhikāra). || 2 ||
This category, named Pati, is proclaimed as the first;
it is characterized by the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, and is thoroughly adorned by the support of Māyā. (3)

Those which consist of action and knowledge, and those which are clearly manifest as the paths of Dharma— this second category, known as "power" (śakti), is defined as the category of "accomplishment" (saṃpad).
Those beings who are always known as the reality of existence, the illusions, and the knives— this third section, consisting of these entities, is for the accomplishment of Śiva.
O bull among sages, he who is the independent animal, the enjoyer, the field-possessor, and the male animal— clearly, he is the fourth among the animals that are the objects of experience.
Those known as the fruition of merit and demerit have come here to experience [their results] while remaining [in this state];
they exist in mutual relationship with one another through the condition of the proven and the means of proof.
But for the fifth, the object to be understood is that which is designated as "enjoyment" (bhoga);
these are the mantras situated on the pure path, such as Śivabhaṭṭāraka and others.
Those who have been liberated shall be filled with power, as shall those objects that were previously forgotten;
this three-stepped ladder is the cause for the deliverance from saṃsāra.
The sixth [chapter] has been declared in this tantra, the Padārthaparameśvara;
[it concerns] perception, inference, verbal testimony, along with analogy. (10)
Presumption (arthāpatti) and non-existence (abhāva) are traditionally recorded as the six means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Among these, that which is perceived through causes such as the sense organs is here called direct perception (pratyakṣa).
The cognition of a sign through a sign is remembered as inference (anumāna). That which is to be understood through the words of a reliable person is called verbal testimony (śabda). || 12 ||

Because it is understood through similarity and so forth, it is indeed proclaimed as "simile" (upamā); for example, from the statement "there is eating during the day," it is understood that "there is none at night. (13)
In the absence of delusion, knowledge itself is proclaimed as non-existence;
thus, through such means of valid cognition, that which is difficult to perceive is remembered as Śiva. (14)
It is said that there are six divisions of the limbs; therefore, it is called "six-limbed" (ṣaḍaṅga).
The limbs and their subdivisions are traditionally held to consist of thirty-six divisions.
The limb of Śiva, the limb of Bhūta, and likewise the limb of Kūṭa;
the limb of Vidyā, the limb of Śakti, and likewise the general limb. || 16 ||

One should worship the Lord upon the body of Śiva, performing the installation and all other rites in every way; or one may worship the Lord upon the bodies of the Bhūtas, performing the installation and everything else in every respect.
O child, the purification of the elements beginning with the feet is indeed performed by means of the limbs of the elements;
having joined them with the names of the *aṇus*, one should practice with the limbs of the elements.
One should perform the expiation with the *kūṭāṅgas* and the *vidyāṅgas*;
at the time of the installation of the *śaktis*, one should perform it with the *śaktyaṅgas*.
For all other deities, one should employ the common limbs;
thus, *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vauṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *ṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* arise.
(91) Those of cruel birth are cruel, while those of peaceful birth are peaceful.
In the case of cruel births, there is "huṃ phaṭ"; the remaining ones are proclaimed to be peaceful. || 21 ||
The elemental self, the inner self, the essential self known as the individual soul (jīva), the mantra-self, and the supreme self—thus it is established in sixfold form. || 22 ||
The elemental self (bhūtātmā) arises from the conjunction of elements; the principle-self (tattvātmā) is established in the principles;
the mantra-self (mantrātmā) is to be known as that which is joined with mantras; and the inner self (antarātmā) is endowed with speech. || 23 ||
The enjoyer of pleasures and pains, abiding in Prakṛti and endowed with the qualities (guṇas), is the individual soul (jīva); however, that which is liberated from these is known as the Supreme.
When he himself is joined with the mind, he is joined with the senses;
consequently, the senses always proceed toward their respective objects. (25)
O Guha, sattva is the illuminating state, while rajas has passion as its essence;
from that, it produces the state characterized by delusion in embodied beings. (26)
One whose self has become such as this is called "Puruṣa";
he is the one who sets in motion the speech of that sound which exists within. || 27 ||
Through the union of prāṇa and apāna, the Sottarātman is proclaimed;
indeed, the five subtle elements (tanmātras), as well as the mind and the ego (ahaṅkāra), are subtle. || 28 ||

The eightfold intellect (buddhi) is to be known, as well as the unmanifest (avyakta), the quality of the person (pauruṣa), the constituent parts (kalā), time (kāla), as well as Māyā, Vidyā, and Vidyeśvara. || 29 ||
(92) Likewise, from the conjunction of these very principles— from Sadāśiva down to the twenty-eighth— Puruṣa is traditionally said to be the essence of the principles (tattvātmā). || 30 ||
The body is all-pervading, subtle, ancient, eternal, and firm; it is the pervader of all principles, unborn, unmanifest, and beginningless.
Not independent and bound, consisting of pure consciousness yet defiled by impurity, deluded, ever-wandering, possessing limited knowledge, lacking sovereignty, and devoid of action. || 32 ||
The mantra belongs to the practitioner alone through the distinction between the signified and the signifier;
here, the essence of the mantra is traditionally held to be the Person (Puruṣa) in his gross, subtle, and supreme forms.
The gross is said to be sound; the subtle consists of thought;
that which is devoid of thought is proclaimed as the supreme.
Know that the gross is verbal, while the subtle proceeds toward yoga;
the supreme, however, is ultimate liberation, having attained which one does not pass away.
Thus has been described the Puruṣa whose essence is mantra, the accomplisher of all aims;
he is omniscient, omnipresent, peaceful, the self of all, and facing in every direction. (36)
Beyond the senses, without support, subtle, eternal, and imperishable;
perfectly partless, formless, undecaying, all-pervading, and constant. (37)
The Supreme Self is proclaimed to be incomparable and immeasurable;
indeed, the Self, though one, bestows all desires and exists in manifold ways. (38)
Death and other such effects are indeed created by Īśvara;
likewise are lifespan, prosperity, action, knowledge, destruction, and happiness. (39)
Having reached the sixfold [elements] right there, it then enters the womb;
the pair consisting of bone and marrow, along with the triad of paternal elements, indeed [constitute this]. (40)
Skin, flesh, and blood—this triad indeed belongs to the mother; these six are declared to be of the father, and they arise at the end of the body. (41)
The phallic emblem (liṅga) is declared to consist of Īśa, while the womb (yoni) is remembered as consisting of Śakti;
therefore, indeed, this entire world of the moving and the unmoving is the union of Śiva and Śakti.
The Boddha, Kṣapaṇa, Cārvāka, Sāṃkhya, Ākeka, and likewise Mīmāṃsā—these are called the six philosophical systems (darśanas) by the wise. (43)
The Vāruṇa, the Āgneya, the Mānasa,
the Vāyavya, and the Māhendra— thus the bath is declared to be of six kinds.
The Varuṇa bath is performed with water, while the Āgneya bath is performed with ashes;
the Abhiṣecana bath consists of sprinkling with waters while reciting the Sadyojāta and other mantras.
In this same manner, the mantra-bath should also be performed for the Varuṇa and Āgneya baths,
preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma) and mentally reciting the root-mantra.
One should perform a mental bath, for that is prescribed in all circumstances;
one should do so amidst a herd of cows with the dust raised by their hooves.
One should perform the bath with the mantra "pavamāna" and likewise with its protective armor (varman),
while facing eastward with arms raised, in contact with the falling rays of the sun. (48)
The Māhendra bath should be performed by the Lord according to the rite of the seven steps;
likewise [the bath is required] after vomiting, at sunrise, after shaving, and after sexual intercourse.
In the case of a bad dream or contact with a wicked person, bathing is prescribed among six [purificatory acts]:
the morning twilight prayer, the recitation of mantras, the fire sacrifice, Vedic study, and the libation to the ancestors. (50)

The worship of the Vaiśvadeva and the guest, as well as the six daily duties, should be performed day after day—especially during the time of worship, at the time of recitation (japa), at the fire sacrifice (homa), and when voiding excrement. || 51 ||
Silence is prescribed during the six [occasions], including the times of bathing and eating.
Now, Śiva, who is born from the body of the cow, [is worshipped] according to the rite of the six limbs.
When worshipped at the *liṅga*, he quickly becomes well-pleased with men.
[One should offer] the cow-dung, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), urine, milk, curd, and ghee of cows. (53)
The six limbs are pure and bestow all accomplishments;
on the heads of the cows are the Gaṅgā and other rivers, proclaiming the sacred mantras.
All the gods are established there, having resorted to the limbs of Tamas;
therefore, by means of the six products born from the body of the cow, beginning with urine and ending with the bile (rocanā), [one should perform the rite].
One should especially perform the worship of Śiva with substances dear to Śiva;
likewise, at night, [offerings] that are sweet, bitter, astringent, and salty [are appropriate]. (56)
And pungent—these are said to be the six flavors born of the elements.
[The worship of] the Sun, the Self, the deity, the Liṅga, Fire, the Guru, and the Book; 57.
Thus has been fully described the eternal worship of Śiva, consisting of the six supports (ṣaḍādhāra),
as well as infinite dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty.
And the lotus—these six are the seats arising from the six;
namely, Gomukha, Svastika, Padma, and Ardhacandraka. (59)
The sixfold posture has been declared as Vīra, Yogāsana, Svastika, Sarvatobhadra, and Gaurītilaka. (60)
The Pārvatīkānta, likewise the Liṅgābja and the Svastika,
as well as the Latāliṅgodbhava— thus the maṇḍala is remembered as being of six kinds.
One should stretch out five lines, with one oriented toward the east and four toward the north.
Know that one *liṅga* is equal to one *pada*, and the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is indeed three *padas*.
One should adorn the face, which is endowed with four marks, with colors;
in its center, however, there should be the white color, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus the Svastika has been described; now the Sarvatobhadra is being explained.
In each of the eight-eighths [sections], there is a lotus; in the outer quarter of four parts, there is a path (vīthī) surrounded by space (vyoma);
and in the six parts, there is a courtyard (ācāra) in the directions of Indra and the others.
In each corner, six [squares] are placed on all sides; this is declared to be the Sarvatobhadra [mandala]. || 64½ ||
For the Sarvatobhadra alone bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (65)
The stainless Gaurī-tilaka consists of seventeen threads;
it has a white central square of four units and four liṅgas in the four directions.
The Liṅga-pīṭha, the Kamala, the Karṇa, and the Kamala-pīṭhaka—
these sixty-four [sections] at the end of the Yuga are here arranged in sequence by groups of six quarters.
Having further adorned the face with colors using the words of the Goddess and the Vedas,
one should arrange ear-ornaments of various colors in the intermediate directions.
In each of all the corners, one should gradually fashion twenty-five squares using various beautiful colors for the creepers.
The Gaurī-tilaka has been described as bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it consists of thirty-two squares, with lines extending toward the east and the north.
In its center, however, is a lotus joined with eight times eight squares;
outside of that, there are three types of pedestals (pīṭhas), and outside of those, according to the rule.
The exit [of the path] should be discolored, while the wise one [should depict it] with various variegated colors;
the other parts, up to the lotus, should be adorned with white colors.
The lingas are black in color, while the doors are colored with various hues;
this [form] of the beloved of Pārvatī is suitable for all ritual acts.
One should draw twenty-six lines of arrangement, with the tips pointing east and north, forming a lotus shape in the center consisting of nine times nine squares. (74)
On the outside, there should be one square unit joined with a pathway in the four directions;
in the center there should be a white lotus, while the pathway is dark blue in color.
At each and every door, one should especially decorate them with various colors:
golden, black, deep red, and likewise white.
One should perform the rite upon the *liṅga* and the *varṇa* with various [mantras], being well-concentrated; indeed, sixteen varieties of *varṇa*-distinctions are prescribed for the eight *liṅgas*.
In each corner, the ritual procedure is prescribed; a white lotus is to be fashioned, and one should sprinkle it with water from kuśa grass using the mudrā resembling a conch shell.
The lotus of the liṅga is traditionally known by the name of the maṇḍala;
one should mark out its position with a thread made of cotton and flour of śāli rice.
One should lay out thirty-three squares starting from the east and ending at the west;
likewise, the north-south line shall also consist of thirty-three [squares]. (80)
Furthermore, one should arrange twenty thousand lines of verses joined together;
therein, in the center of thirty-six single-word units, one should fashion a lotus.
It should be provided with eight petals, radiant with a pericarp and filaments;
indeed, one should fashion the filaments using one-third of that [pericarp] portion.
One should draw the pericarp with yellow color and the filaments with red color;
at its base and at its tip, one should draw it with white color. (83)
Encircled by a pericarp and endowed with white and red [colors],
one should likewise draw eight petals, red in color, along with a white line.
Its end is to be known as black; it is remembered that what has occurred is white.
In the east is the saffron liṅga, and in the south is the black liṅga.

One should meditate on the golden liṅga in the north and the white liṅga in the west; starting from the southeast (āgneya), one should visualize them with creepers according to their respective colors.
Thus, the maṇḍala arising from the liṅga is prescribed as the Sarvatobhadra for Brahmins, while for a king it is the Gaurīlatā.
For Vaiśyas, however, the creeper-sign (latāliṅga) [is prescribed], and for Śūdras, it should be the svastika.
There is worship with a mandala for a month, and so forth, throughout the six seasons beginning with spring. || 88 ||
Spring, likewise summer, and after that the rainy season;
then winter and the cool season—these are declared to be the six seasons. (89)
In spring, there should be the Svastikābja; in summer, the Sarvabhadraka;
in the rainy season, the Bhadra is prescribed, as well as the Liṅgābja and the Svastika.
In the autumn, however, Pārvatī [worships] the circle of her beloved;
it is declared to be a lotus in the winter, and specifically a svastika in the month of Śaśira (Mārgaśīrṣa). || 91 ||
(99) When the [sacrifice] takes place on a single day, the worship is performed starting from Aries and ending with Pisces;
having propitiated the six maṇḍalas, one should also consecrate the ritual substances. || 92 ||
The Mahāmaṇḍala-saṃjña, however, reaches the heart of Śiva;
it is recommended for the rite of purification (pavitrārohaṇa) and especially for initiation (dīkṣā). || 93 ||
Through the worship of the great maṇḍala, one attains all desires;
at the conclusion of the vows, the wise man should worship the lotus of the liṅga. (94)
And when the extraction of the *liṅga* must be performed, especially during the rite of penance,
one should then prepare a nine-naved diagram for the purpose of the consecration of the preceptor (*ācārya*).
Of all rites performed for specific desires as well, the nine-naved lotus is the bestower of fruit. || 95½ ||
Candra and Aśvinī, Sthāṇu and Śitāṃśu— this pair belonging to Śiva— is in the pitcher (kumbha), on the head, the ear, and the throat;
and the two feet are in the foot-support of the eight-part pitcher.
And from the emission of the future, [he attains] the single stage. || 96½ ||
Thus ends the sixth canto.
Now begins the seventh canto.
The self-manifested (svayambhū), the divine (daivika), the celestial (divya), the human (mānuṣa), the ṛṣi-made (ārṣaka), and the Rākṣasa— the Bāṇaliṅga is said to be the sevenfold liṅga.
Impurity (*mala*) is also to be known as sevenfold: delusion (*moha*), pride (*mada*), attachment (*rāga*), another called despondency (*viṣāda*), and likewise heat (*tāpa*) as the remainder. (2)
The diversity of all these impurities is also proclaimed;
herein, the impurity called delusion (moha) is innate and beginningless for human beings.
He who, due to his preeminence among those seated with pride and the like, is the best of the twice-born;
