he in whom delusion regarding women and other objects arises even for himself. (4)
That is known as delusion (moha), by which, through the failure to distinguish between what is to be avoided and what is not,
even a woman who has been obtained becomes another's wife.
"She is surely a celestial maiden"—thus is pride described by the wise;
for by it, even when being rebuked, his pride increased manifold.
One who has attained the inability to abandon [attachment] is said to possess passion (rāga), because in its absence there arises dejection and tearful eyes. (7)
That which is called the stain of despondency arises from the extreme suffering of living beings; it is an internal torment for the ascetic, manifesting as extensive lamentation within the self. (8)

That is known as *tāpa* (fever), and from that, the remaining impurity (*mala*) arises; when the *madhyātman* (the intermediate self) is within it, the state of being possessed by impurity and so forth is extremely difficult to overcome.
"This is Bandhīri's wife; if this great chariot-race were false, then I would have achieved my purpose, or else who could be the savior of my own? (10)
(101) That stain which causes such thoughts as these regarding the family for men, and which produces various delusions, is indeed a manifold and false reality. || 11 ||
These seven are declared to be the innate impurities (mala) of men who possess impurity;
even when these exist, there are the bonds derived from Māyā and the perishable Kalās.
With its power intensified by that, it experiences the qualities born of nature;
first the equinox of the vital breath, and likewise the equinox of the mantra. (13)
The *nāḍikā-viṣuva*, the subsequent *praśānta-viṣuva*, the fifth, the *śānti-viṣuva*, and likewise the *kālasya-viṣuva*. || 14 ||
They know the seventh, the consciousness of Śiva called *laya*, as the equinox (*viṣuva*);
the *praṇava* is the heart-mantra, and the equinox is the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
Within the channel [nāḍī] is the dvādaśānta, and likewise the tranquil Kuṇḍalī;
at the end of Śakti is Samanā, and within Śakti is Kāla, ending with Unmanā.
That indeed is declared to be the equinox (viṣuva); beyond that is what is designated as the channel (nāḍī).
The conjunctions of the disciple’s self, vital breath, and mind are designated as the vital breath (prāṇa). 17.
Having meditated upon the dissolution within the center of one's own belly,
one should contemplate the conjunction and separation of the phonemes beginning with *ta*, *ka*, and *u*.
From the heart up to the cavity [of the head], that which is designated as the mantra is the equinox (viṣuva).
Above the penis are the kanda and the navel; the heart is located from the pit of the throat.
The tip of the throat, the middle of the eyebrows, the forehead, the aperture of Brahmā, the Śakti, and the End of the Twelve— these are the ten knots in sequence. (20)
Having abandoned the root mantra through the triple purity, the resonance (nāda) proceeds;
from the complete union with the channel of resonance, that is considered the equinox of the channels (nāḍīviṣuva).
Having sequentially abandoned the phonemes *a* and *ā*, the phoneme *ma* known as the *bindu*, and those known as *nāda* and *nādānta* within Brahmā and the others respectively; || 22 ||
In the seventh [cakra], within the Śakti, one should lead the disciple’s self to dissolution;
one should know that to be the state of perfect peace, wherein the sphere of activity is stilled.
When the Nāda has entered the middle of Śakti, it flows as far as the end of the Samāna;
that is declared to be the Viṣuva of Śakti, known by the name of the Unmanī-time.

Having meditated upon this sevenfold equinox (viṣuva) within the supreme abode of the qualified authority—which is designated as the principle (tattva)—the best of teachers [performs] the equinox. || 25 ||
Above that is the mass of consciousness (cidghana), the eternal power endowed with all qualities, which transcends the cause of the mind and is free from rebirth. || 26 ||
Having gradually brought the self to dissolution, one should cause the full [breaths] to descend;
these are the [channels] previously mentioned that sport within the body of Sadāśiva. (27)
The four forms [of the Lord] are those who desire liberation through initiation, bathing, and recitation;
or they are those who have been joined [to the path] by means of initiation endowed with the power and strength of yoga. || 28 ||
Know, O lords of sages, that they all sport with subtle manifestations like Sadāśiva himself; yet they are not the Lords of Causes.
They have not yet attained the state of Śiva; their dharma is now being described.
They are considered to be those who reside in proximity [to liberation], dwell in peace, and possess exclusive knowledge (jñānakevalins). || 30 ||

The atoms that abide in the principle known as Sādākhya are remembered as both those characterized by desire and those characterized by cessation, as well as those possessing form and those devoid of form. (31)
Even those who possess a physical body yet have attained absolute liberation (mūrtikevalins) are proclaimed as Rudras due to their wrath;
thus, this sevenfold liberation has been described in its various divisions.
Among these, one is supreme, subtle, the sphere of both cause and effect,
transcendent, perfectly complete, independent, and facing in all directions.
One is established in his own nature as being without a lord; the other six are considered lords. They perform the five cosmic functions by the command and appointment of the Lord (Patih).
In that regard, their resolve concerning creation and so forth occurs in such a way that it is equal for all;
indeed, there is no inequality in their resolve because of their state of being established in that Truth.
Even those who have attained that state through the yoga of authentic Śaiva practice,
having reached the bliss that lasts until the end of existence, proceed to the supreme state.
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śaktimān, Rakṣāparvata, Vindhya, and Pāriyātra—these seven are the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas). || 37 ||
The seven oceans, well-known in their respective order as salt, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and water, increase twofold in each successive one. (38)
Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmalī, Gomeda, and Puṣkaradvīpa—these seven great continents are said to be separated by oceans. (39)

In the Śāka [kalpa], when the Śāka tree has reached its highest height, the one whose name is bound to the Śāka tree shall worship the self-existent Brahmā in the golden lotus within the heart-lake. (40)
On Mount Krauñca, at Hemakundara, the Dātya was slain by Krauñca,
after he had fought for a long time with the highly skillful Krauñca, who possessed wonderful powers of illusion.
And because of that wonderful deed of tearing open the belly of that Daitya named Khāta,
he was called Krauñca by name, even though his original name was Ketu.
In Śālmala there is a śālmali tree made of gold with a thousand pillars;
it is dear to the immortals, its banner is that [tree], and it is the basis for its name. (43)
On Gomeda, the king named Gomati, who was devoted to truth, ruled;
he was the patron of those who were like Bhadra and Agni in their ritual fire, and his lineage was characterized by silence and meditation. 44.
While these were engaged in the sacrifice for Hari,
Gautama, out of anger, chose him as his preceptor, requesting that he be free from rivals and possess imperishable Soma.
O Sage, the cows were burnt by the fire of the ascetic’s anger within the sacrificial enclosure;
from their fat, a great desire was severed, and thus the Gomedha gem came into being.
There are rivers called Puṣkariṇī, adorned with golden lotuses;
by that [lake], that Puṣkaradvīpa is proclaimed, frequented by the gods. (47)
O lady of beautiful countenance, he is known as Agnidhṛta in Jambūdvīpa;
in Śākadvīpa his name is Medhātithi, and in the island named Kuśa, he is Vasu.
And on Krauñca, King Jyotiṣmān resides; on Śālmalī, Dundubha is remembered;
on Gomedha, Havyavāha; and likewise, the Vasus are on Puṣkara.
I shall now state individually the names of the Ādityas for each of the Śāka, Gomedha, and Vāsina periods, which last for a duration equal to the Tretā Yuga.
Gāyatrī, Bṛhatī, Uṣṇik, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti,
Anuṣṭubh, and Triṣṭubh— these, O Hari, are said to be the meters (chandas) of you, O Hara.
Śveta, Harita, Jīmūta, Lohita,
Vaidyuta, Mānasa, and Suprabha— these indeed are the seven clouds.
Āvāha, pravāha, and likewise the next, anuvāha; then saṃvāha, vivāha, and above that shall be parāvāha. (53)
Likewise, above that, the wind carries seven rims upward;
[the beings of] the fourth [rim] are beasts like deer and birds, and the reptiles.
From the immobile [beings] comes the human and the divine; indeed, these are the seven wombs.
One should know that the Vināyaka has a short tail and is like a deer. 55.
Those with long tails below are declared to be the species of domestic animals; those with two wings they call "winged," and those that crawl are called "reptiles. (56)
Those beings who speak with speech are proclaimed as "men" (nara);
likewise, the immobile is called "established," as is the world of divine origin. || 57 ||
Māgadhī, Āvantikā, Prācyā, Śaurasenī, Māgadhī, Bāhlīkā, and Dākṣiṇātyā—these are proclaimed as the seven languages. (58)
Excavation, extraction, burning, filling, dwelling with cattle, and [using] what is left over by Brahmins, as well as products of the cow—these seven are the purifications of a site. (59)

When rubbing stone against stone, or earth against earth, one should dig a pit seven finger-breadths deep for the sake of purification; likewise, when using brick or lime, one should avoid a pit of one span.

One should employ water in these seven instances: during the invocation, in the arghya vessels, at the time of bathing, likewise at the time of sipping water (ācamana), at the offering of food, and at the dismissal.
I shall explain the wheel of worship (pūjācakra) correctly and in due order:
the master of ablution (snānācārya), the performer of the hooded rite (phaṇīkarmī), the initiate (samayī), and the lord of the observance (samayādhipa).
The ruler of the country and the one belonging to his own land—these seven are the leaders of the wheel.
It is endowed with five faces and adorned with seven tongues of flame.
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, and then Suprabhā,
Atiraktā, and Bahurūpā— these are proclaimed as the seven tongues of fire.
(107) Three are situated above, three are situated below, and the remaining are in order from the east onwards.
I shall now duly explain the limbs of the vow (*vratāṅga*) in their proper sequence. 65.
The girdle, the tooth-stick, the antelope skin, the triple staff, the twilight prayers, the sacred fires, and alms-gathering—these they know as the seven forms [of the student]. (66)
O fair-faced one, these seven items, beginning with the girdle, which are seen as restraints, should be practiced by the student at the time of initiation.
Bhūteśa, Pāśupatya, the Gaṇas, and Gaṇeśvara, Unmattaka, Auṣadhāna, and Vrateśa is remembered as the seventh. || 68 ||
These seven are the observed vows for those practicing celibacy (brahmacārins):
the Aṣṭakā, the Śrāddha on the festival day, and likewise the Śrāvaṇī rite on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa.
The Caitrī and the Āśvayujī [full-moon sacrifices] are to be known; these seven are the Pākayajñas.
Following those are the Ādhāna (consecration of the fires), the Agnihotra, and the Darśa.
The Paurṇamāsa sacrifice is to be known, as well as the Cāturmāsya;
the Paśubandha has been specified, and after this, the Sautrāmaṇi.
The Haviḥ-yajña has been fully described; these seven are remembered as purifiers. The Agniṣṭoma is prescribed for the rites concerning the fire, and the Ṣoḍaśaka is likewise prescribed.
The Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma as the seventh—these are declared to be the Soma sacrifices;
one should purify oneself at the time of initiation (dīkṣā). || 73 ||

In this system, there are seven categories: the threefold soul (jīva), the threefold non-soul (ajīva), as well as both influx (āsrava) and restraint (saṃvara), shedding (nirjarā), bondage (bandha), and liberation (mokṣa). (74)
And indeed, marked by the doctrine of manifold aspects (syādvāda), all things are non-absolutistic in reality. (74½)
Thus ends the seventh chapter.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
The Samaliṅga, the Vartamāna, the Śaivādhikya, the Svastika, the Sarvatobhadra-liṅga, and the Sarvadeśika. || 1 ||
The Dhārā-liṅga and the Mukha-liṅga—thus the liṅga becomes eightfold.
O Lord of Śacī, I shall now tell you the names of the pīṭhas in their entirety.
The first is named Kalā, the second is Payodhara;
the third may also be [so called], while the fourth is designated as Vajra.
The fifth is known as Indrā, and the sixth shall be Amṛtā;
Saṃvarta is the seventh, while the eighth is called Keśanāndika.
The measurement of the liṅga, the womb (garbha), the door-pillars, the bolt, and the cubit-measure in finger-breadths—these eight are said by the makers to constitute length. || 5 ||
The teacher should have the craftsmen fashion [the image] according to the desired measurement; because all its limbs are visible, it is called a "pratimā" (image). (6)
Wherever images have been installed in a temple,
one should determine their placement according to the prescribed measurements, whether from the door or from the feet.
In the portion consisting of the quality of obstruction (tamas), this seat is the element of space (ākāśa).
There may be a distinction of eight types of jeweled liṅgas, and likewise those made of metal.
Māṇikya, coral, lapis lazuli, and likewise crystal; diamond, emerald, sapphire, and the Puṣyarāga born of gems.
The ruby (māṇikya) should be known as bestowing prosperity; the coral (pravāla) brings subjugation;
the lapis lazuli (vaiḍūrya) leads to the attainment of sons; and the crystal (sphaṭika) grants all perfections.
The blue gem bestows wealth and grain; the topaz grants enjoyment;
that which is called diamond brings attraction; and likewise, the emerald provides nourishment.
From pearls, there shall be all success; such is the fruit of those born from gems.
One should fashion a linga made of gems measuring from one finger-breadth up to a full cubit.
The pedestal for the jewel-liṅga should be made according to its own proportions, joined with a rounded top that corresponds to its length. 13.
Thus has the [liṅga] made of jewels been described; now the liṅga made of metal is being declared:
gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, and brass. (14)
Iron, lead, tin, and that which is born of copper;
gold is to be known as bestowing prosperity, and silver as granting royal success. (15)
Copper bestows sons, while bell-metal (kāṃsya) causes enmity;
brass (dvārakūṭa) effects eradication, and iron is for the destruction of enemies.
Lead removes disease and increases the lifespan of the three cities;
Ananta, Sūkṣma, and Ekanetraka are those spoken by Śiva. (17)
One should worship Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin;
from Ananta up to Śikhaṇḍin, one should worship the eight Vidyeśvaras.
Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra, Bhīma, and Mahādeva—thus the eight forms have been proclaimed. (19)
To those Rudras who swell with power and offer salutations in these places,
the Lord whose body consists of eight forms bestows the supreme state.
The Sun, Water, Earth, Wind, Fire, Space,
the initiated Brāhmaṇa, and the Moon— these are the eight forms (mūrtis).
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
intellect, mind, and ego—this is declared to be the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka).

The City (Purī) exists within the embodied form and the mere elements; she is the internal cause of the qualities (guṇas), the creative power (māyā), and the eightfold group of subtle bodies beginning with Kalā.
111) Now, therefore, I shall briefly declare the eight qualities that belong exclusively to the self: compassion toward all beings, patience, and freedom from envy; || 24 ||
Purity, lack of exertion, auspiciousness, and thereafter freedom from miserliness and lack of longing—these are remembered as the eight qualities of the self (ātma-guṇas). || 25 ||
In the presence of the God of gods, he should address his well-disciplined disciples:
"O initiated one, you must always enter even the Śiva-scripture. (26)
One should not step over the shadow of the preceptor or of one’s elders, nor should one step over the shadow of a linga, nor indeed the shadow of the temple of the Lord. || 27 ||
A woman has no initiation without her husband; she should never have sexual union with other women;
she should not consume the remains of offerings (nirmālya); and she should not revile the devotees of Śiva. (28)
Thus, one should reveal these eight pledges to the initiate;
then the expansion of the intellect is brought forth by means of the sublime Dharma. (29)
That which is knowledge, dispassion, and likewise supreme sovereignty; as well as ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of sovereignty. (30)

Driven by the desire for enjoyment, the intellect (buddhi) is impelled by the eight qualities; directed by the determination of the subtle self (aṇu), it becomes the faculty of ascertainment (adhyavasāyinī). || 31 ||

For the sake of worldly convention, even though there is no difference in the substance [of the clay], jars, pots, and so forth are designated individually and separately according to the difference in their manifestations. (32)
Amareśa and Prabhāsa, Naimiśa and Puṣkara likewise,
Āṣāḍhī, Daṇḍimuṇḍī, Bhārabhautī, and Bhavāntika. (33)
And Lakulīśa is renowned; thus the eight secret [sites] have been declared:
Śrīparvata, Hariścandra, Japyeśvara, and Ārdrātiśeśvara. (24)
Madhyameśa, Mahākāla, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava—this group, beginning with Guhya, is proclaimed as the eightfold secret (Guhyāṣṭaka). || 35 ||
Gaya, Kurukṣetra, Nakhāla, and likewise Nakhala;
Vimala, Aṣṭahāsa, Māhendra, and Bhīma—these are the eight.
The eight most secret [sites] by name, which liberate one from all sins:
Chagalaṇḍa, Dviraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, and Maṇḍaleśvara. (37)
Kālāñjara, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sthūleśvara, and Sthaleśvara—
these constitute the "Pavitra-aṣṭaka" (the group of eight purifiers), which increases great merit.
Vastrapāda, Rudrakoṭi, Ravimukta, Mahālaya, Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, and Dīptimān; || 39 ||
And Sthāṇvīśvara is renowned and celebrated throughout the three worlds;
this group of eight sites is to be known as the highly auspicious Rudrakṣetra. 40.
The Atiguhyāṣṭaka Rudras, as well as the Guhyāṣṭakas, the Guhyādguhyāṣṭaka, and the Pavitrāṣṭaka; || 41 ||
These five—the Sthāṇu and the Aṣṭakās—reside upon the earth as a restraint;
they are established as manifest signs for the sake of favoring the worlds.
O Six-faced One, whatever water is situated near them is a supremely meritorious sacred ford (tīrtha); having bathed there, one shall go to Śiva.
One should point out the sacred fields that are the abodes of Rudra’s incarnations;
all who die here go to the supreme state of Rudra.
This group of five eights should be known as the characteristics of Rudra’s sacred field (rudrakṣetra):
a garden and so forth, a path, a well, a grove, and a temple of the deity. (45)
Whoever should perform [rites] in these places shall obtain imperishable fruit.
This great field of sixty-eight is ordained as the station of the Self-Existent (Svayaṃbhū). || 46 ||
They shall worship the temple, its radiance, the monastery in the assembly hall, and that which belongs to the gods who practice austerity, meditative absorption, and recitation.
One obtains inexhaustible fruit; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Marriage has been declared to be of eight kinds by Śiva, the Supreme Self. (48)
The Brāhma, the Daiva, the Prājāpatya, and likewise the Ārṣa;
the fifth is declared to be the Āsura, as well as the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa. (49)
The Paiśāca [marriage] is to be known as eightfold; indeed, the wise speak of them according to the excellence of age, conduct, character, and lineage. (50)
Having invited [the groom] and given away a maiden along with cattle, land, and gold,
that is designated as *brāhma* and is remembered as the best among marriages. (51)

In sacrifices, the act of giving a daughter to officiating priests (ṛtvijas) is the divine (daivika) form of marriage; likewise, giving her to a Brahmin who possesses wealth and good character and who is seeking a wife. (52)

Having personally performed the fire-sacrifice (homa) and having given garments, ornaments, and earrings according to the prescribed rite, that which is thus bestowed is remembered as the *prājāpatya* gift.
Having given his own daughter along with a pair of cattle, or even a single pair of cattle, this is remembered as the Ārṣa form of marriage. (54)
Having adorned the girl with ornaments and repeatedly entreated her mother, and having given wealth to her kinsmen, that which follows is the formal taking of the bride. (55)
Likewise, it should be known as "suram" by the learned, according to the accepted doctrine;
this applies when both [the man and woman] engage in union out of passion. (56)
Thus has his gift been described; it is recited as being of the Gandharva type, having performed a great and terrible battle with blows from the palms and slaps. (57)
This Rākṣasa [form of marriage] consists of forcibly abducting a weeping maiden;
whereas that which is taken by stealth when she is asleep or intoxicated is the Caurya [form]. (58)
The Paiśāca [form of marriage] is to be known as having been proclaimed previously as being preceded by five water-libations;
however, among those, the first four are for the high-souled Brāhmaṇa.
One should perform the *āsura* rite or other such rites, while avoiding three others:
the *garbha*, the *puṃsavana*, the *sīmantonnayana*, and the *jātakarman*. (60)

Through the completion of the naming ceremony, the rite of emerging from the birth chamber, the first feeding of solid food, and the tonsure ceremony—by these, O Goddess, one is then born as a twice-born (dvija). (61)
Or the best of teachers may perform the eightfold rite separately according to the tantra:
the seizing of the ground, the installation of the child, and the first brick.
The foundation, the head, the bricks, the abode, the installation of the liṅga, and likewise the consecration—these are proclaimed as the eight limbs in their proper sequence. (63)
Water for the feet, water for sipping, the respectful offering (arghya), fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the food offering—this is proclaimed as the eightfold offering (aṣṭāṅga). || 64 ||
One should worship the Supreme Lord with the eightfold offering:
water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, rice grains, flowers, and sesame seeds. (65)
The eightfold *arghya* is thus proclaimed, together with barley and white mustard seeds;
it is used for the vessels of invocation and *arghya*, as well as for bathing, incense, and unguents.
In the offering of food (naivedya) and in the ritual dismissal (visarga), one should employ eight flowers:
the arka, the lotus, the bilva, the nandyāvarta, and the pāṭalī.
The karavīra, campaka, and blue lotus— the eight [flowers] for the temple—
[should be placed] on the crown of the head, at the neck, at the heart, and at the navel and the private parts.

One should likewise worship the two knee-ornaments and the two sandals with the eight flowers; the seat is worshipped with the root-mantra, the form-mantra, and the limb-mantras, while the eight-flower offering is performed excluding the eye-mantras. (69)

For those who are impoverished and without protectors, for children, women, and fools, for those addicted to enjoyments, for those satisfied with disease, and likewise for those whose souls are absorbed in meditation— 70.

The "Eightfold Flower Offering" has been described for those who are devoted to the Śiva scriptures, whose souls are intent on various spiritual accomplishments, and who are both attached and detached.
It is used when beginning the ritual impressions (vāsana), at the commencement of the bath, and at its conclusion;
likewise during the time of incense, at the beginning of the sacrificial oblation (havis), and similarly at its end. || 72 ||
At the conclusion of the dance festival, at the end of the dance, one should strike the bell eight times;
in the Rudra-field with the Heart-mantra, and likewise in a river, at a landing-place, or on a mountain peak.
On the horns of a bull, however, or on the tusk of an elephant, there may be eight types of earth;
likewise, there are ghoṣa, kha-svana, śabda, sphoṭa, nāda, and dhvani.
The resonance (jhaṃkāra), the upward movement, and indeed the sound itself are recorded as the eighth;
thus, the group of eight consisting of the signs of realization beginning with the balance (tulā) has been proclaimed.
The balance, water, poison, the sacred vessel (kośa), the heated gold coin (taptamāṣa), and thereafter rice and the footprint—these are the eight ordeals in their proper sequence. (76)
In all temples of Śiva, and in the temples of Durgā and Sūrya;
in the abodes of Vināyaka and Guha, in the midst of rivers, and on their two banks.
Or one may perform it on the bank of a pond in the presence of the king and Brahmins,
at all times except for the periods of the two doors and the two suns. (78)

The restraints (yama), the observances (niyama), and the postures (āsana); thereafter, breath control (prāṇāyāma); then withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), meditation (dhyāna), concentration (dhāraṇā), and finally absorption (samādhi). || 79 ||
This should be known as the eightfold means for yogis to achieve yoga:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from impurity. (80)
In that regard, purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord constitute the fivefold observance (niyama). || 81 ||
The cow-faced (gomukha), the svastika, and others are proclaimed as the postures for sitting; having assumed one of these, one should then practice yoga. (82)
For the sake of yoga, first perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) for him:
exhaling is called recaka, and likewise, inhaling is called pūraka.
One should practice the three [breaths] through restraint by means of the *praṇava* (Om).
When the senses are established in their respective objects, one remains steady. (84)
The state of remaining for as long as possible is called withdrawal (pratyāhāra);
having conceived the objects according to their true nature within the substrates (ādhāras). (85)
Retention is said to be on the support, while concentration is that which is supported;
one should understand the eight limbs of yoga as the remover of all suffering. (86)
(118) Aṇimā, mahimā, laghimā, and likewise garimā; prākāmya, īśitva, and vaśitva—these [powers] arise from the principle of Śiva (śivatattva). || 87 ||
One may cast off from the body whatever gross thing one desires, even down to the size of an atom;
and because one obtains [powers] even as small as an atom, it is called *aṇiman*. (88)
Because one reaches the region of the root-syllable as if traveling a thousand [yojanas] by one's own will, it is therefore known as *laghimā* (levity). || 89 ||
Having made the earth comparable to a forest, it is worshipped by those who dwell in hymns of praise;
because it is worshipped everywhere, therefore that [earth] shall possess greatness. (90)
The attainment of all substances is declared to be their acquisition (*prāpti*); while mastery (*prākāmya*) consists in the power of entry into bodies. (91)
The attainment of the abodes of the Sun and others is declared to be their lordship; yet, it is precisely because of that lordship over those [abodes] that their lordship is established. (92)
Through union with Śiva and proximity to Him, that state is known as "Śivatva";
the yogi especially attains the eightfold supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇiman*. (93)
Omniscience, sovereignty, and indeed the status of being the creator of the world; as well as stainlessness, eternity, and likewise the quality of bestowing grace upon all. || 94 ||
Sovereignty and lordship, as well as the eight qualities of Śiva; || 94½ ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter.
(p. 119) || Now begins the ninth chapter. ||
The partless (niṣkala) is indeed fourfold, and the manifest (sakala) is likewise;
that which is a mixture of both parts and the partless is therefore both manifest and partless.

One should know that the entire [manifest] form is the Flower (puṣpa), while the Scent (gandha) therein is partless (niṣkala). That which is supreme is said to be partless, whereas the other is possessed of parts (sakala). || 2 ||
Thus it is declared as both supreme and inferior; it may be with parts (sakala) or without parts (niṣkala).
That which is without parts is the place of dissolution, while that which has parts pertains to the sphere of authority.

In this way, both would constitute enjoyment; one who possesses the authority over both dissolution and enjoyment, having known that which is higher than the highest, becomes liberated and a destroyer of bonds. || 4 ||
These nine principles have been proclaimed as bestowing liberation upon devotees:
Śiva, Śakti, Nāda, Bindu, Sādākhya, Īśvara, and Rudra. || 5 ||
Viṣṇu is their grandfather; the origin of each one is now described. From the Śiva-tattva, by a thousandth part, the Śakti-tattva arises.
And from that very thousandth part arises the principle of Nāda;
and from that very thousandth part arises the principle of Bindu.
Therefore, by a tenth part plus one, [one attains] the reality known as Sādākhya;
from that, by a tenth part plus one, arises the state of Īśvara.
It is said that Rudra arises from a thousandth part of Īśvara;
and Viṣṇu likewise arises from a ten-millionth part of Īśvara. (9)
The origin of Brahmā is from a ten-millionth part of Īśvara;
Īśvara is traditionally known as the Lord over creation, dissolution, and preservation.
Everything has arisen from Brahmā; the protection of all is performed by Viṣṇu;
and the total destruction of the worlds is accomplished by Śiva, the Supreme Lord.
Just as [the power] arose from Śambhu, so too is the emergence of Śakti;
the first is declared to be Ādhāra, and the second is Svādhiṣṭhāna.
The third is Maṇipūra, and the fourth is Anāhata;
the fifth, known as Viśuddha, one should apply at the root of the throat. (13)
The action [lotus] is at the root of the palate, endowed with divine nectar;
situated between the two bows is the seventh, the orb of knowledge.
The forehead is declared to be the eighth, endowed with two [lotuses] within the lunar disc;
above that is the Brahma-aperture (brahmarandhra), which is here called the ninth support (navādhāra).
The deities residing in the nine supports, in successive order as far as the Avani [support], are Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti. (16)
One should meditate upon the Śāntyatītā, Kriyāśakti, Jñānaśakti, and likewise Icchāśakti and Parāśakti within the nine streams.
The principle of the Self (ātmatattva), and Vidyā, and immediately thereafter the principle of Śiva;
Maheśvara, Sādākhya, and after that, Bindu. || 18 ||
One should meditate upon these in sequence as Nāda, Śakti, and Dānta:
Marīci, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu. (19)
Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha created these through the science of yoga;
indeed, they are called the "nine Brāhmaṇas" in the Purāṇas.
Now, [I shall describe] specifically the names and forms of the aforementioned numbers of fires, as well as their respective seats of worship.
I shall describe them in order, O Mahāsena, for the sake of the Lord of Creatures, in nine ways:
one should know Śivāgni as the first and Vṛddhyāgni as the second. || 22 ||
The third is the Gārhapatya fire, the fourth is the Āhavanīya fire,
the fifth is the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, and the sixth is the Yauvanāgni fire.
The seventh is the solitary fire (kevalāgni), and the eighth is the child-fire (bālāgni);
the common fire (sāmānyāgni) is the ninth; thus the varieties of fire have been proclaimed. || 24 ||
One should understand the distinction of names and the form of the rays in their proper order:
the Heart of Sadāśiva is the very nature of Śiva and Śakti. (25)
There is no difference between the two, just as there is none between the wind and the sky;
through the union of Śiva and Śakti, the Mother is Śakti and the Grandfather is Śiva. (26)
Therefore, with every effort, the arising of Agni is proclaimed during the times of consecration, festivals, and likewise at the time of initiation. (27)

One should employ the "child-fire" for festivals, the "youthful-fire" for the purpose of consecration, and the "aged-fire" for daily rites; a wise man may also perform other sacrifices with these fires.
For auspicious rites such as marriage and the like, the Gārhapatya fire is prescribed;
for rites connected with the ancestors, one should employ the Dakṣiṇāgni.
In all rites for the gods, there should be the Āhavanīya fire;
O Brahmin, listen with a concentrated mind as I describe how one should prepare the Śiva-fire therein.
He is endowed with five faces, red in color, adorned with seven tongues, possessing ten hands and three eyes, and decorated with all ornaments. || 31 ||
Clad in red garments and seated upon a lotus,
he sits in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana) and is endowed with ten weapons.
Kanaka, Bahurūpā, and Atiriktā after that;
then Suprabhā, Kṛṣṇā, Raktā, and another, Hiraṇmayī. (33)

The three [fires] are situated with their faces turned upwards; the remaining ones are situated in the directions starting from the east: Devakī in the east, Pitṛyā in the south, and Gārhapatya shall be in the southern fire-chamber.
Then, indeed, their Āhavanīya fire was proclaimed by those mantras as being red in color,
with two eyes, one face, and four arms.
Clad in white garments and adorned with all ornaments,
one of those [three] is endowed with three feet, standing with one [foot] bent upward. (36)
The right hand should hold the gesture of protection (abhaya), while the left is joined with the gesture of granting boons (varada);
it is highly recommended that the two implements, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, be held in the hands. (37)
He should have the form of a fierce being mounted upon a ram, accompanied by the Sūktas;
thus, O wise one, the true nature of the Gārhapatya fire is described.
O Four-faced One, I shall describe the form of the Āhavanīya fire, preceded by its manifestation from a thousandth part of the Dakṣiṇāgni.
Having two faces and three feet, joined with two nostrils, endowed with three girdles, possessing six eyes, and having a tawny radiance. (40)
Mounted upon a bull with four horns, possessing hair like the rising sun,
and endowed with seven tongues arranged in the order from right to left.
In the right face there are four tongues, and likewise three in the left face;
in the right side there are four hands, and Agnijihvā is on the left side.
In his left hands he holds a sacrificial ladle (sruk), a small spoon (sruva), a rosary, and a spear; and in his right hands he holds a javelin, a fan, and a vessel of clarified butter.
Thus, after [describing] the Āhavanīya fire, the Dakṣiṇāgni is now described:
it has two faces and six arms, its cord is white, and its faces are both white and black.
(124) He is endowed with a crown of matted locks, has six eyes, and a tawny radiance; he has a fierce gaze, a massive body, and a face slightly smiling. (45)
Furthermore, he holds the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and a sword in his right hands,
while in his left hands he holds the boon-granting gesture (*varada*), a tuft of grass (*kūrca*), and a skull-cup (*kapāla*).
The Gārhapatya fire is mounted upon a bull, has three feet, and its form is accompanied by Svāhā;
it belongs to householders, while the Dakṣiṇāgni belongs to the ancestors.
It should be offered with divine hymns, and it is established for others as well;
these are proclaimed in sequence as the child, the youth, and the old age [of the fire]. (48)
The nature of the Dakṣiṇāgni is now described as the Yauvanāgni;
from a thousandth part of the Dakṣiṇāgni, the Kevalāgni originated.

He has two eyes and two arms, joined with the staff, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness; he is clothed in white garments and possesses a luster equal to the color white. || 50 ||
That which is known as *kevalāgni* is now described as *bālāgni*;
from a thousandth part of *kevalāgni*, *mahānasa* arises. (51)
He has one face and two arms, is mounted upon a ram or a bull,
is clad in red garments, and is endowed with three tufts of hair.
He has four horns and three eyes, and a sacrificial ladle (sruva) should be in his right hand;
he possesses outstretched arms, is white-limbed, and holds a wooden spoon (darvī) in his hand.
O Grandfather, he who is known as Mahānasa is of manifest form; [he embodies] the erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the heroic, the furious, and the terrifying sentiments. (54)
The loathsome, the furious, and the peaceful, as well as the nine dramatic sentiments (rasas), arise; from the erotic arises the comic, and from the furious arises the pathetic sentiment.
The heroic is known to arise from the same [source], as are the loathsome and the terrifying;
the peaceful and the independent are thus described by dancers as the aesthetic sentiments (rasa) and emotional states (bhāva). || 56 ||

The permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva), when brought to a state of being relished through the determinants (vibhāvas), the consequents (anubhāvas), the involuntary emotions (sāttvikas), and the transitory emotions (vyabhicāris), is known as rasa. 57.
First is the Ānanda-tāṇḍava, after that the Kālī-nṛtta,
then the one known as Saṃdhyā-tāṇḍava, and after that the Munigrahaṇa.
Then there is the dance known as Gaurītāṇḍava, followed by the Saṃhāratāṇḍava;
after that, the Tripuratāṇḍava, and likewise the Bhujaṅgalalita. || 59 ||
Then follows the begging for alms; these constitute the nine [limbs] of the Tāṇḍava dance.
[The rites are performed] at the commencement of the removal of the used floral offerings (nirmālya), at the commencement of the ritual bath, and at its conclusion.

One should strike the great bell at the time of incense, at the beginning of the oblation and other rites, at the end, near the daily festival, and at the conclusion of the dance; however, one should strike it during the nine periods.
Thus ends the ninth canto.
(p. 126) || Now begins the tenth chapter. ||
Damidā, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (caru), parched grain (lāja), mustard seeds, barley, sesame seeds, bamboo shoots, mung beans, and rice— these are said here to be the ten substances.
Or, with the *śamī* tree and the *sadyojāta* mantra, clarified butter (*ājya*) is offered;
with the *aghora* mantra, one offers the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and with the *puruṣa* mantra, parched grain (*lāja*). || 2 ||
One should offer mustard seeds with the Īśa-mantra, barley with the Hṛdaya-mantra,
sesame seeds with the Śikhā-mantra, and a bamboo staff with the Kavaca-mantra.
One should offer mung beans with the Netra-mantra and rice with the Astra-mantra,
either one hundred and eight times, or fifty, or twenty-five.
Having offered the materials specifically prepared for the rite,
the wise practitioner should offer the Vyāhṛtis at the end of each material and at the end of each mantra.
There, one who has mastered the four Vedas should perform the study;
having recited the mantra of the temple, he should especially recite the hymn of praise.

The fuel-sticks (samidh) should have their tips like a finger; the middle finger's length is the medium size, while the best is said to be one kalāngula in height—such are the characteristics of the dimensions of the fuel-sticks.
Having prepared one *karṣa*, half a *karṣa*, and two or three *karṣas* respectively,
one should then perform the oblation of clarified butter (*ghṛtāhuti*) according to the sequence starting from the highest quality.
Then, one should offer the *vyāhṛti* oblation with the measure of a full *sruva* ladle; thereafter,
one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) until the cavity of the *sruc* ladle is completely filled.
Then the preceptor should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Śiva-mantra;
thereafter, having worshipped the fire and sprinkled it, he should cause it to be extinguished.
The preceptor himself should perform the principal oblations according to the prescribed rite;
his sons or his disciple may perform them, or one may have the oblations offered by another.
At the conclusion of the oblation, one should offer the sacrificial food; through the oblations, it becomes the āhuti-offerings for prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna.
Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—these are known as the ten winds; likewise, hear now about the ten channels (nāḍīs). || 13 ||
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, as well as Suṣumnā;
Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā, and Pūṣā and Yaśasvinī. (14)
Alampūṣā, Kuhu, and Śaṅkhinī, which consists of ten nāḍīs—these are the ten principal channels among all the channels. || 15 ||
The channels, beginning with the iḍā, are likewise distributed throughout that body;
then, the vital air (vāyu) moves sequentially through the midst of those channels.
The great channel named Kuṇḍalī is proclaimed to be in the center of the navel;
it is eight-fold and circular, like a sleeping serpent.
Above the navel there is a lotus, like the lotus of a pond as described before;
situated in its center is the individual soul (jīva), possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns. (18)
Within that, it is declared, are the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire;
situated in their midst is the God, possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns.
On the left side is the iḍā channel, and on the right side is the piṅgalā channel;
the suṣumnā is in the middle channel, extending as far as the thumb.
Gāndhārī is in the right eye and Hastijihvā in the left;
Pūṣan is indeed in the right ear and Yaśasvin in the left ear.
Alaṃpūṣā is located at the end of the penis, and Kuhu is situated in the anus; Śaṅkhinī is in the middle of the navel, while the ten channels (daśanāḍī) are established [there]. || 22 ||
All the channels without exception revolve around the body like a wheel;
because it revolves like a wheel, the channel is here called "cakrin" (the wheeled one).
A trident, an axe in hand, a sword and noose, as well as a lotus,
a bell, an elephant, fire, and a razor— these are his ten weapons.
Standing at a height of one tāla above the *bhūta*s, one should construct it with all measurements according to the measurement of the *bhūta-avabhūta*.
Whatever color is stated for a weapon, its name shall be of that same color.
Thus have the ten weapons held in the hands of Sadāśiva been described.
In all auspicious rites, during festivals, and in the act of processions,
one should especially worship the weapons of the world-protectors (lokapālas). (27)

Now, [the following] is the tenfold characteristic of Dharma: *hiṃsā* (non-violence), *satya* (truthfulness), the threefold restraint of the senses, charity, self-restraint, austerity, and meditation. || 28 ||
I shall now describe [the means] for binding the body:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, freedom from impurity, absence of anger, service to the guru, purity, contentment, and straightforwardness. (29)
Thus, the tenfold dharma has been declared by those who are most excellent in performing dharma:
cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, clarified butter, clothing, grain, and molasses.
They say silver is salt; thus, in sequence, are the ten grains:
knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, austerity, truth, forbearance, and fortitude. (31)
Having joined to himself the state of being the creator as well as the state of being the presiding controller,
these ten imperishable qualities abide eternally in Śaṅkara.
Through the procedure of initiation (dīkṣā), the manifestation of the syllables of the Śikṣā occurs;
by means of the manifestation of the bath and the sacred ash, it directly reveals liberation.
The first is the nature of reality; the second is the vision of reality; the third is the purification of reality; and the fourth is the form of reality. (34)
The fifth is the manifestation of the self, the sixth is the purification of the self;
the seventh consists of the forms of Śiva, and the eighth is the vision of Śiva.
The ninth is Śivayoga, and the tenth is Śivarūpaka. || 36 ||
Thus ends the tenth canto.
The lexicon named Paryāyamañjarī, composed by Nigamajñānadeva—the disciple of the yogin Nigama-jñānaśiva, a resident of Puṇḍarīkapura—is hereby complete.
